practices.title: Join clips with a short audio crossfade at one sample rate
practices.rule: Join clip audio with a short crossfade and resample everything once to a common rate (48 kHz is the video standard) before the join.

practices.how: acrossfade with a duration of tens of milliseconds, then loudnorm on the whole.

practices.title: Score face identity with embeddings, and calibrate on your own footage
practices.rule: Where the character has a real or realistic face, add a numeric check: cosine similarity of face embeddings (ArcFace) between sampled frames and the approved reference, with a threshold set from your own good and bad takes.
practices.why: Embedding distances separate real video (ArcFace 0.08) from generated video (0.17 to 0.48 across models); there is no universal cutoff and numbers are not tied to human judgement.
practices.how: Detect the face in 5 to 8 frames, skip frames with no face, take the minimum and the mean similarity; flag takes below the calibrated line and send them to the VLM check.

practices.title: With a start picture, prompt only the change
practices.rule: When the generator gets a start picture, write only what moves and what the camera does, and do not redescribe what the picture already shows.

practices.title: Chain clips from the last frame, and check the join

sources.title: 3D claymation AI prompts
claims: Pair positive material words with a ban list such as no photorealism, no smooth 3D rendering, no CGI polish; positive-only prompts let photorealism leak back.
Name the material (polymer clay), visible thumbprints, seams, and matte not shiny; smooth seamless forms read as CGI.
Light like a small set: one practical lamp, hard shadow edges; soft diffuse light breaks the miniature look.
Ask for a 12fps feel, held poses and no motion blur; omitting motion words gives smooth interpolation.
Build the set from craft materials (felt, cardboard, foam-core) with visible set edges.
sources.notes: Vendor blog; no measured comparison.

sources.title: Claymation AI video
claims: Name the material (plasticine, clay, felt) and a miniature set; handmade nouns give a handmade result.
Include 12fps and words like stepped or slightly jittery for a choppy stop-motion rhythm.
Keep camera moves small: locked camera or gentle pan.
Each run gives a few seconds; make several takes and keep the one where the clay moves best.
Close inspection can still reveal the clip is AI-generated.
sources.notes: Vendor page.

sources.title: Claymation AI: how creators fake stop-motion TikToks
claims: Prompt structure: character or scene, setting, action, texture, lighting, camera, frame-rate feel, style reference, set, aspect ratio.
Generate 3 to 5 variations per prompt because texture quality varies a lot between rolls.
Suggested a still reference first to lock the character, dropping motion language from that still.
Claims model strengths (Veo 3 texture, Sora 2 lighting, Kling facial expression, Seedance still animation); unmeasured.
Clay reads warm and nostalgic and clashes with sleek, urgent or B2B subjects.
sources.notes: Marketing blog; model rankings are the author claim.

sources.title: AI stop motion generator
claims: Material names produce distinct looks: clay, felt, paper craft, wooden puppet, plastic figures.
Ask for visible fingerprints, handmade imperfections, slight wobble, and a miniature set or diorama.
Use studio lighting words (warm studio, dramatic side light) not natural outdoor light.
Output is not true frame-by-frame animation; it mimics the look and approximates real craft.
sources.notes: Vendor page; gives no fps control.

sources.title: How to make clay animation with AI
claims: Words like smooth, glossy, perfect, polished pull results toward a clean 3D render; use handmade, imperfect, matte.
Say clay, not just stop motion: stop motion also covers cut-outs and puppets.
Formula: character + action + setting + texture + lighting + motion; one action per shot.
Paste one fixed character description word for word into every scene; two or three memorable details hold best.
First attempts often look close but too smooth, and characters shift between scenes.
sources.notes: Vendor tutorial.

sources.title: How to create looping claymation fantasy video with AI
claims: Four-part prompt: subject, material, motion, aesthetic; generate 5 to 8 second segments and reuse the same wording.
If too smooth, ask for imperfect pacing, a frame rate that wanders between 8 and 15 fps.
Material cues: fingerprints, visible armature wire at joints, glossy eyes on a matte body; visible set glue seams.
Loops work best at 5 to 8 seconds; past about 8 seconds closing the loop gets harder.
Without material and motion detail the output looks like smooth CGI.
sources.notes: Vendor page.

sources.title: 12 principles of animation and how to use them in AI video
claims: Write the lead-in beat into the prompt (she glances down and takes a breath before jumping) so the clip has anticipation.
Describe motion as a curved path rather than a straight move to get arcs.
Ask for hair or loose clothing to keep moving after the body stops; models often freeze these.
Models often skip follow through, solid drawing, and slow in and slow out; first generations look too linear.
A stylised look (cartoon, chibi) permits bigger poses than a realistic one; keyframe workflows give more timing control.
sources.notes: Vendor blog; principles mapping is the author own method, untested.

sources.title: How do you stop AI from drifting into photorealism
claims: Reuse one style block on every prompt: a positive anchor plus an explicit not live action, not photorealistic line, with concrete texture terms.
Load a batch of style-reference frames once; the page cites 20 to 30 for a short and 64 for a feature.
Extract palette and texture from raw animation references and turn them into words instead of naming the reference.
Without the style block or references in context the model reverts to photorealism.
Generate candidate frames in each style, pick one, and lock it as the anchor.
sources.notes: Vendor FAQ.

sources.title: How I handled character consistency in AI cartoon video generation
claims: Style drift (face, clothing, art style changing between scenes) is the core cartoon problem.
Two routes: reference video as identity anchor plus script, or one still image plus a motion description.
Complex or multi-character scenes need several attempts; no metrics given.
sources.notes: Single user, promotes a tool; claims unverified.

sources.title: How to create consistent characters across AI-generated kids videos
claims: Example duckling has few traits: round shape, one signature colour, big eyes, one accessory; few distinct traits are easier to repeat.
Cast each recurring character once as a reference sheet and load it instead of retyping descriptions.
Switching visual style between episodes undoes consistency even with the same cast.
Fix off-model scenes at the reference level, not by re-describing in text; keep one aspect ratio per series.
sources.notes: Product marketing; the simplicity point is partly inferred from the example.

sources.title: Paper cutout animation AI videos
claims: Name the traits: flat layered card, snipped edges, visible construction-paper grain, soft shadows between layers.
Paper cutout is a flat layered form of stop motion; use the exact words paper cutout to steer away from clay.
One concrete set and one jointed character per scene; flat sideways pan or gentle drift.
Reuse the same character description in every prompt.
sources.notes: Vendor page; no clip limits stated.

sources.title: How to create educational videos for kids with AI
claims: Pacing table: ages 3 to 5 a new concept every 30 to 60 seconds, episodes of 2 to 5 minutes, very slow narration and gentle fades.
Use bright cartoon or illustrated styles rather than photorealistic for young children; bold primary colours for ages 3 to 4.
Avoid abrupt scene changes, flashing effects, loud or jarring audio; check for eerie faces or unnatural animal poses.
Run a sound-off test: a child should follow the visuals without audio.
Several short videos beat one long one.
sources.notes: Vendor article; its retention figures are unsourced.

sources.title: The 12 principles of animation
claims: Squash and stretch conveys weight, heavier in cartoon looks and subtler in realistic work.
Anticipation is a small preparatory move (a crouch before a jump) that makes the action readable.
Follow through and overlapping action: parts keep moving after the main action stops, at different rates.
Slow in and slow out, arcs and timing: motion eases and curves, and frame count between poses sets weight and mood.
Appeal does not mean pretty: a distinctive quirk makes a character memorable.

sources.title: Illustration and art styles in Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse
claims: Animating on twos holds each drawing two frames, an effective 12 fps inside a 24 fps film.
The film mixed ones and twos by character and scene: Miles on twos for staccato motion, Peter on ones for fluid motion.
Smears: several copies of an object along its path replace digital motion blur.
Halftones and misaligned colour recall offset comic printing; a team built the look through style frames and tests.
sources.notes: Frame-rate assignment per character is commentary, not a studio statement.

sources.title: Animation principles
claims: Timing is the number of frames between poses: fewer is quick, more suggests weight.
Slow in and out: frames are denser at the start and end of a move.
Squash and stretch keeps volume constant while deforming.
Staging directs attention to the key element with composition, contrast and angle.

sources.title: Stop motion AI videos
claims: Core cues: felt, wire armature, paper-craft, wood; visible craft texture and seams; slight frame-by-frame stutter.
Describe character, set and camera together; example is a felt puppet in a handmade miniature village.
The page does not say how precisely stutter or fps can be controlled.
sources.notes: Vendor page.

sources.title: Character Mixing for Video Generation
claims: Names style delusion: when cartoon and realistic characters share a scene, realistic ones turn cartoonish or the reverse.
Proposes cross-character embedding and augmentation trained on mixed-style data.
Reports gains on a benchmark of cartoon and live-action series with 10 characters; abstract gives no numbers.

sources.title: Veo 3 animation guide 2026
claims: Name the animation style early and commit to one dominant style; two equal styles give muddy results.
Flat 2D: say flat 2D, bold outlines, limited colour palette. 3D: 3D rendered, soft rim lighting.
Repeat the full character description every prompt and keep the style phrase identical; cartoon versus illustrated causes drift.
Weak points: lip sync to recorded dialogue and precise consistency over many shots.
sources.notes: Third-party blog, not Google.

sources.title: How to create mixed-media videos with AI
claims: Pull stills from footage, restyle only the first still, approve it, then apply the look to the rest.
Restate the same palette and mark style in each request and compare neighbouring frames.
Keep original footage for moments where a face or product must stay exact.
One texture and one recurring motif are easier to repeat than a busy mix.

claims: A LoRA for Stable Diffusion XL that gives stop-motion and claymation imagery; examples name Laika and plasticine.

License is listed as other; check the CivitAI source.

sources.title: How to make animated videos
claims: Turn a style reference into an editable written description (texture, colour, lighting) and pass it into every generation step.
Wire one character reference into every generation instead of re-describing; build a multi-angle sheet first.
Approve key frames as stills before animating; stills are cheaper to reject than video.
When a shot drifts, regenerate from the closest reference angle; review the whole sequence cut to cut.

sources.title: How do you keep AI-generated video shots visually consistent
claims: Write a style block (medium, explicit negatives, palette, lighting) and prefix every prompt with it.
Keep prompt order and vocabulary fixed across shots.
Approve the opening still of each scene before generating motion.
Reported roughly three generations per usable shot and about a quarter of clips used.
Fix drift in the reference panel and regenerate only the affected shot.

claims: Write a master character description and reuse it verbatim with the same terms and one prompt order: character, scene, style.

claims: Name flat-design 2D forms, bold geometric shapes, minimal or no shading; ask for solid colour blocks with no gradients and crisp edges.

Lock shape language, palette and proportions in a character card and reference it in every prompt.

claims: Add no gradients, no shadows to keep the look flat; example style words: minimalist vector, clean outlines, high contrast.

Favour bold silhouettes and simple geometry and skip micro-detail; lock line weight and corner radius for a set.

Stop-motion is valued today for its handmade physical quality.

Fuses video and audio with joint attention and injects text through cross-attention to balance the two inputs.

sources.title: Veo (Google DeepMind model page)

sources.title: Kling 2.6 Review and Prompt Guide for Perfect Native Audio Sync

Tag speakers ([Character A]) and add a tone note; two-speaker exchanges are most reliable, three or more blend voices.
With many voice instructions speech can drift after about 5 to 6 s; native speech is English and Chinese, others are translated.
Use 10 s for dialogue, 5 s for ambient or SFX clips; 10 s max; draft with audio off because audio doubles credit cost.
Voice Control in image-to-video binds a voice to a character as [Character@VoiceName].

sources.title: How to keep an AI voice consistent across every video clip
claims: Lock one voice source or voice ID per character and never swap tools mid-series.

Generate all of one character's lines in one session on the same settings so drift shows at once.
Use audio tags such as [whispers] for one beat instead of loosening stability for a whole scene.

sources.title: Seedance complete guide: audio and video generation
claims: Put dialogue in its own block naming speaker, language and tone; each line can use its own language.

Sound effects bind to on-screen events at frame level, so describe the action that makes the sound; you can state "no music".
Lists English, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, Spanish, Indonesian plus regional Chinese dialects.

sources.title: LTX-2: Efficient Joint Audio-Visual Foundation Model

Asymmetric dual-stream transformer: 14B video stream, 5B audio stream, bidirectional cross-attention.

sources.title: OmniHuman-1: Rethinking the Scaling-Up of One-Stage Conditioned Human Animation Models
claims: Animates a single image from audio, video or both; handles portrait to full body.
Supports speech and singing and human-object interaction.
Mixing several motion conditions in training is how the authors enlarge usable data.

sources.title: LatentSync: Taming Audio-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Models for Lip Sync
claims: Audio-conditioned diffusion lip sync is weak because models take a shortcut and ignore the audio-lip link.
SyncNet supervision plus a more stable SyncNet raised its accuracy on HDTF from 91% to 94%.
TREPA aligns temporal representations to keep frames consistent.

sources.title: ACE-Step: A Step Towards Music Generation Foundation Model
claims: Open diffusion music model: up to 4 minutes in about 20 s on an A100.
Supports lyric editing, remixing, voice cloning and track generation per the authors.
About 15 times faster than LLM-based music baselines.

sources.title: FFmpeg filters documentation (acrossfade, loudnorm, sidechaincompress, adelay)
claims: acrossfade overlaps two streams by a set duration (default 44100 samples), with selectable curves.
loudnorm defaults: integrated -24, LRA 7, true peak -2; two-pass use needs measured_I, LRA, TP, thresh.
sidechaincompress defaults: threshold 0.125, ratio 2, attack 20 ms, release 250 ms; used to duck music under speech.
adelay delays channels by milliseconds by default.

sources.title: Text to speech (ElevenLabs docs)
claims: Output is not deterministic; the seed helps but small differences remain.

sources.title: Timed Text Style Guide: General Requirements
claims: Minimum 5/6 of a second per subtitle event (20 frames at 24 fps), maximum 7 seconds.

Keep articles with nouns and names together on a line.

claims: Lists ElevenLabs speech models, speech-to-speech, dubbing, voice isolation and sound effects as separate audio models.

claims: Audio tags go in square brackets, e.g. [whispers], and some may be spoken as sound effects, so test.

Phone numbers, dates and units can be mispronounced; expand them in the text first.
Speed range is 0.7 to 1.2; extremes may hurt quality.

sources.title: WebVTT: The Web Video Text Tracks Format
claims: Timestamps use a full stop before three millisecond digits; hours are optional.

sources.title: SubRip (SRT) file format

sources.title: Sound effects (ElevenLabs docs)

Meant for dubbing and localization from one recording.

claims: Wan 2.5 makes voice, ambience and lip sync in one pass and can take an uploaded voice track.
Audio language follows the prompt language; Chinese prompts reported most reliable.
Clips up to 10 s at 24 fps in most sources.
sources.notes: Search summary only.

sources.title: Veo 3 native audio prompt guide 2026
claims: Says "no music" is the one negative worth including because unrequested soundtrack is the most common failure.
sources.notes: Search summary only; low trust.

sources.title: Use reference images to guide video generation (Veo on Vertex AI)
claims: Veo 3.1 takes one to three subject reference images (referenceType asset), JPEG or PNG; the images should show a single person, character or product.
With subject images veo-3.1-generate-001 returns 8 second videos only; aspect 16:9 or 9:16.
The page gives no advice on angles, lighting or image quality for references.

sources.title: Magic Mirror: ID-Preserved Video Generation in Video Diffusion Transformers
claims: Uses a dual-branch face extractor (identity plus structure) and a light adapter with Conditioned Adaptive Normalization on a video DiT.
Two-stage training: synthetic identity pairs first, then video data; claims identity kept with dynamic motion and few extra parameters.

sources.title: ID-Animator: Zero-Shot Identity-Preserving Human Video Generation
claims: A face adapter on a frozen video backbone makes a person video from a single reference face image, with no per-subject training.
Trained with a random-reference strategy and an ID-preserving loss; works with community AnimateDiff backbones.

sources.title: Stand-In: A Lightweight and Plug-and-Play Identity Control for Video Generation
sources.publisher: Bowen Xue et al. (WeChat Vision, Tencent; Nankai University)
claims: Adds a conditional image branch to a pretrained video model; identity is steered by restricted self-attention with conditional position mapping.
About 1% extra parameters and about 2,000 training pairs; claims better identity and quality than full-parameter training.
Extends to face swap, pose-referenced and stylised generation.
sources.notes: Title and authors corrected after an independent search on 2026-11-08 (the first entry had the title from memory). The abstract describes the ~1% extra parameters; the training-pair count was not re-checked. Built on Wan2.1-14B text-to-video.

sources.title: IP-Adapter: Text Compatible Image Prompt Adapter for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
claims: A 22M-parameter adapter with decoupled cross-attention (separate paths for text and image features) on a frozen diffusion model.
Because the base model is frozen it works with custom models of the same base and with other control tools; image and text prompts combine.

sources.title: InstantID: Zero-shot Identity-Preserving Generation in Seconds
claims: Needs one face image and no per-subject training; an IdentityNet combines face embedding, landmark image and text.
Works with SD1.5 and SDXL community models in one forward pass; avoids the storage and tuning cost of LoRA, DreamBooth and textual inversion.

sources.title: PuLID: Pure and Lightning ID Customization via Contrastive Alignment
claims: Tuning-free ID insertion that trains with a contrastive alignment loss plus an ID loss so the base model's behaviour is disturbed as little as possible.
Claims background, lighting, composition and style stay close to the output without the identity inserted.

sources.title: FLUX.1 Kontext: Flow Matching for In-Context Image Generation and Editing in Latent Space
claims: The authors say earlier editing models lose character consistency and stability over several editing turns, and that Kontext keeps characters better in iterative edits.
Evidence is their own KontextBench (1,026 image-prompt pairs, five task types including character reference); no failure cases are listed in the abstract.

sources.title: Concat-ID: Towards Universal Identity-Preserving Video Synthesis
claims: Encodes the reference image with the VAE and concatenates its features with the video latents along the sequence axis; reuses 3D self-attention, no extra modules.
Claims to beat prior methods for single and multiple identities and to extend to virtual try-on and background control.

sources.title: DreamBooth: Fine Tuning Text-to-Image Diffusion Models for Subject-Driven Generation
claims: Fine-tunes a text-to-image model on a few images of a subject so a unique identifier binds to it, with a class prior-preservation loss.
The tuned subject can then appear in new scenes, poses, views and lighting not in the reference images.

sources.title: Omni Reference (--oref)
claims: --oref takes a reference image of a character, object, vehicle or non-human creature; --ow weight runs 0 to 1000, default 100.
Use about 25 for style changes (photo to anime) and about 400 to keep a face or clothing; do not go above moderate values without very high --stylize or --exp.
At low weight, describe the features to keep in detail; two references for two characters is called somewhat untested.

sources.title: Kling Element Library user guide
claims: A multi-image element is one main image plus 1 to 3 extras (2 to 4 total); the main image should be front-facing for higher consistency.
A video character element is a 3 to 8 second clip of one character, ideally with several angles; subject types include characters, animals, items, costumes, scenes.
Tips: give each element a unique name, describe core traits and what to ignore, add more angles for multi-view consistency, bind elements that appear in the start frame.

sources.title: KLING VIDEO O1 user guide
claims: Up to 7 images or elements without a video input, 4 with a video; images JPG/PNG, at least 300 px, up to 10 MB; an element holds up to 4 images of one subject.
Refer to inputs in the prompt with @Image, @Video and @Element; describe each element, then interactions, environment, lighting.
For consistency: build elements from several angles, reuse the library across shots, reference every character explicitly in every prompt, keep lighting and style direction constant.

sources.title: Ray3 Modify user guide
claims: Modify swaps the character in an input video (max 10 s) for a character reference image; the reference adapts to the video's style and lighting.
Strength runs from Adhere (keep shapes, good for retexture) to Reimagine (looser, for stylised or non-human characters); at the top the edges and background blur.
Reference mode works better at 1080p; the reference is called image1 or cref in prompts.

sources.title: How to prompt Gemini 2.5 Flash Image generation for the best results
claims: If a character's features drift after many edits, start a new conversation and give a detailed description of the character.
For targeted edits, name only the element to change and say everything else stays the same.
With several input images of different aspect ratios the output takes the ratio of the last image.

sources.title: Image generation with Gemini (Nano Banana)
claims: Up to 14 reference images per request: Gemini 3 Pro Image takes up to 5 character images, 6 object images and 3 style images; the 3.1 Flash models up to 4 characters and 10 objects.
The lightest model is stated as not optimised for multiple reference inputs or multi-turn editing.
sources.notes: Only the first 100,000 characters of the page were read.

sources.title: FLUX.1 Kontext image editing
claims: Kontext is said to hold character consistency over multiple edits; the example makes one change per prompt and refers to the subject by pronoun.
Scene changes such as place or weather are separate steps; output size follows the input (multiples of 32); a fixed seed gives repeatable results.
The page now recommends FLUX.2 for new projects, citing better editing and multi-reference support.

sources.title: How do I create and use a Soul ID character
claims: Train on 20 to 80 photos of one person: varied angles and expressions, well lit, at least one full-height shot; no sunglasses, hats over the face, heavy shadow, crops or repeated poses.
A smaller clean varied set beats a large inconsistent set.
Result is the same person, not pixel-identical; extreme styles or odd angles drift slightly; one Soul ID is one person, so use Elements for several characters.

sources.title: How many angles should a character reference sheet have
claims: Suggests six panels: front, side, profile, back, a face close-up and a mid-angle close-up, at 4K; the minimum for a simple character is a headshot plus a full-body view.
Remove props from the hands before the turnaround, generate several options and lock one before any video; make a new sheet for each look change.
Close-ups keep small details (scars, accessories) because video models invent what they cannot see.
sources.notes: Vendor guide; one small team reportedly used 11 reference images for 4 characters and 1 prop.

sources.title: Generate character turnarounds
claims: Prompt shape: style, then character description (features, outfit, expression), then a technical line such as 'character design sheet with multiple views (front, side, back), consistent lighting across all views'.
For complex characters make the front first, refine it, then use it as the reference for side and back views; keep pose influence 70 to 100 for aligned views.
Fix small inconsistencies in faces, hands or outfit with masking and inpainting.

sources.title: How to use Veo 3.1 Ingredients to Video
claims: Up to three references (subject, environment, style); pick images of 1080p or more with a clean subject outline and an uncluttered background.
If the face drifts, the references may be too similar: use different angles (front and side profile); add explicit traits such as hair and eye colour to the prompt.
sources.notes: Third-party guide, not Google.

sources.title: AI video character consistency: keep the same face across every scene
claims: Use 3 to 5 references (front, three-quarter, profile) at 1024 px or more, same lighting and outfit across them, clean background.
Write a style guide (hair, eyes, build, skin, clothing, marks), repeat key features in every prompt, state what stays the same, and specify outfits because unspecified clothing gets improvised.
Change one variable per scene transition; save the best take early; repeated re-rolls accumulate variation, so stop after about 3 to 4.

sources.title: The Build #1: How to create consistent AI characters
claims: Define age, face shape, hair, skin tone, wardrobe, posture precisely; vague definitions let the model improvise and drift starts.
Reuse the same phrasing, attribute order and vocabulary in every prompt; build a neutral turnaround (close-up, front, side, three-quarter, back) on a plain background.

sources.title: Build consistent AI characters for video in 4 steps
claims: Make a hero image first, then one still per scene from it as a subject reference; animate each still in short 3 to 8 second clips and keep the best of four outputs.
Reusable description block: type, colours and texture, signature details, pose and framing, lighting and style.

sources.title: Why AI video models fail when two characters interact
claims: When two characters share a frame the model blends face, hair and build into one hybrid.

Fix order: make characters visibly different (height, palette, body shape, costume silhouette), use multi-reference input (Kling up to four images), sketch the contact pose, film a rough mock, or cut together takes.
Reported budget: about three generations per usable shot and roughly 25% of takes used.
sources.notes: Vendor FAQ with a creative director quoted.

sources.title: Why start/end frame methods do not keep characters consistent
claims: Each generation is a fresh sample: start and end frames are loose guidance and faces, outfits and small props drift between clips.

Lock multi-angle sheets first (about five generations per lock); make a new sheet when outfit or injury changes; chain by giving the prior clip, character references and an environment plate together.
sources.notes: Vendor FAQ.

sources.title: Training a FLUX LoRA: dataset, captions and settings
claims: For a person or character use 15 to 30 sharp images; the model learns what stays constant, so vary backgrounds, lighting, distance and angle on purpose.
Short sentence captions with a rare trigger token; describe what varies (clothing, setting) and leave out the features to be learned.

About 50 to 100 steps per image; save checkpoints every few hundred steps; overfitting shows as repeated pose or background and failure to change clothing, fixed by an earlier checkpoint or LoRA weight 0.7 to 1.0.

sources.title: How to fine-tune Wan 2.2 with an API
claims: Use at least 10 on-subject images or clips with a same-name .txt caption each; trim video clips to about 5 s; do not upscale source above 720p.
Default 400 steps and learning rate 0.0002; a rare trigger token in every caption; compare scale 0 and 1 on the same seed; try scale 0.6 to 0.9 if overbaked.
sources.notes: Describes a generic subject or style trainer, not specifically characters.

sources.title: The Chosen One: Consistent Characters in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
claims: Generates a batch from a text prompt, finds the group with a shared identity, extracts a tighter identity from it and repeats, with no reference images.
Claims a better balance of prompt fidelity and identity consistency than baselines, supported by a user study.
sources.notes: Search summary (not the abstract) adds runtime of about 20 min per character and failure to keep supporting characters consistent.

sources.title: MAGREF: Masked Guidance for Any-Reference Video Generation
claims: Several reference images go in through region-aware masks and channel concatenation; text-derived subject semantics are injected per region to cut confusion between subjects.
A four-stage data pipeline with varied training pairs targets copy-paste artifacts.

sources.title: Video Storyboarding: Multi-Shot Character Consistency for Text-to-Video Generation
claims: Self-attention query features control identity as well as layout, so motion cannot be transferred without also transferring some identity.
A training-free Q-injection keeps identity across shots; later paper versions emphasise motion transfer more than multi-shot.

sources.title: Lights, Camera, Consistency: A Multistage Pipeline for Character-Stable AI Video Stories
claims: Pipeline: an LLM writes a production script, a text-to-image model makes consistent character visuals, a video model uses them as anchors per scene.
Ablation: removing the visual anchors drops the consistency score from 7.99 to 0.55 (scale not given in the abstract).
sources.notes: Under review; v1 only.

sources.title: Identity-Preserving Image-to-Video Generation via Reward-Guided Optimization (IPRO)
claims: Image-to-video models lose the input person's identity with large expression change, big motion or a small face in frame.
Tunes the model with a face identity score as reward, with a KL regulariser; tested on Wan 2.2 I2V.

sources.title: Slot-ID: identity from a reference video clip
claims: Single reference images give face deformation, identity drift and over-smoothed faces, because one image cannot show how identity changes over views and expressions.
Uses a short reference clip to distil identity tokens, with an image anchor; biggest gains under hard pose, expression and motion.
sources.notes: Title shortened from the abstract page; the abstract does not use the phrase pose-locking.

sources.title: EchoVideo: Identity-Preserving Human Video Generation by Multimodal Feature Fusion
claims: Names copy-paste artifacts and low similarity as the cost of leaning on low-level facial image information.
Fuses high-level text and identity-image features and randomly uses shallow face features in stage two, to ignore occlusion, pose and lighting of the reference.

sources.title: GroundShot: anchors and visual memory for multi-shot consistency
claims: An entity's first clear appearance is its anchor and sets the consistency ceiling for later shots; drift is the slow divergence of reappearing entities.
Training-free agent: orders shots by usefulness as references, checks an entity before it enters memory, retrieves references before each shot; introduces GroundBench.
sources.notes: Title shortened from the abstract page.

sources.title: SkyReels-A2: Compose Anything in Video Diffusion Transformers
claims: Composes characters, objects and backgrounds from reference images with text; trains on prompt-reference-video triplets with an image-text joint embedding.
Introduces A2 Bench; claims the first open-source commercial-grade elements-to-video model.
sources.notes: Another paper (AnyID) reports in search snippets that SkyReels-A2 copies reference clothing and background; not verified.

sources.title: OpenS2V-Nexus: A Detailed Benchmark and Million-Scale Dataset for Subject-to-Video Generation
claims: OpenS2V-Eval has 180 prompts over seven subject-to-video categories and three automatic metrics: NexusScore (subject consistency), NaturalScore, GmeScore.
Evaluated 18 models; the dataset has 5 million 720p subject-text-video triplets.

sources.title: Aura: Consistent Multi-Subject Video Generation via VLM-Grounded Semantic Alignment
claims: Adds subject-aware RoPE-Shift and learnable tokens to tell subject types apart and reduce copy-paste; a VLM is used as a conditioning encoder.
sources.notes: Search snippets say a frozen VLM judge scores identity consistency and hard-copy per entity on 1 to 5; the abstract page does not show that.

sources.title: Face Consistency Benchmark for GenAI Video
claims: Scores faces with six embedding models via DeepFace: cosine distance of each frame to a reference frame, or 200 random frame pairs; frames with no face are skipped.
ArcFace distance: real video 0.0843, Runway Gen-3 0.2346, HunyuanVideo 0.1734, CogVideoX1.5-5B 0.3005, Vchitect-2.0 0.4843 (lower is better), 30 videos per model.
No correlation with human judgement is reported.

sources.title: Character references for consistent AI output
claims: A text description gives a different face each time; the reference fixes identity and the prompt controls the scene. For Sora 2 do not re-describe the character, it can clash with the reference.
Use a sharp frontal or three-quarter photo with hair and distinctive features visible, 2 to 3 extra views, test 3 to 5 images across scenes before production, reuse the same set.
For outfit consistency name the key garment in the prompt (for example 'wearing the same blue jacket').

sources.title: AI video character consistency workflow
claims: A prompt gives the model a description, a reference gives it evidence; keep the video prompt short and about motion.
Checklist per clip: face shape and hairline, outfit and accessories, light temperature, style finish, whether the face holds through head turns.
Prefers defining a first frame and an end frame over simple last-frame chaining.

sources.title: How to keep characters consistent in AI video
claims: Prompt pattern: a fixed identity line (age, face and hair, signature clothing) unchanged in every prompt, then a variable line for action, camera, setting, light.
Drift fixes: gradual face change means the wording shifted; different look per scene means no anchor reference; distortion in motion means shorten or calm the clip.
Compare every cut to the original reference, not just the previous clip; approve a clip before reusing a frame of it; fix drift before sound and grade.

sources.title: Wan 2.2 prompting guide
claims: For image-to-video describe how things move (motion, camera, environment effects, speed), not what should appear; the image already sets the subject and scene.
Animate only what is visible; keep motion low on clothing; lock elements with anchors such as keeping the face still while hair moves.
sources.notes: Third-party; not Alibaba's own guide.

sources.title: Major identity drift and character consistency failure in video-to-video generation
claims: A user reports 20 to 30 tries in Google Flow where the face became a generic avatar even with a character profile, full-body and profile references attached.
Another user says even simple photo animation starts on the right face and the face changes significantly later; no official answer in the thread.
sources.notes: Anecdotal; the product may have changed since.

sources.title: Training-Free Consistent Text-to-Image Generation (ConsiStory)
claims: Shares internal activations across a batch through a subject-driven shared attention block and feature injection, with no optimisation step.
Claims state-of-the-art subject consistency and text alignment; extends to several subjects.

sources.title: CANVAS: multi-agent storyboarding for long multi-shot narratives
claims: Enforces character continuity, persistent background anchors and location-aware planning; tested on ST-BENCH, ViStoryBench and new HardContinuityBench.
Reports gains over the best baseline of 21.6% background, 9.6% character and 7.6% props consistency.
sources.notes: Title shortened from the abstract page.

sources.title: PersonaShot: benchmarking person-centric narrative continuity in multi-shot video
claims: About 1,000 multi-shot segments, 16 metrics; character coherence tested within shots, across cuts and over sequences.
Finds a clear gap between perceptual quality and cross-shot continuity: visually strong videos reset characters' physical state between shots.
sources.notes: Search summary adds that storyboard-guided systems held identity best; not in the abstract page.

sources.title: OpenAI adds reusable characters and video stitching to Sora
claims: Sora characters extend cameos to pets, illustrations and toys as reusable avatars; the brief gives no creation steps or limits.
sources.notes: Search summaries of other pages report a 3 to 10 second capture clip and two characters per video; not verified.

sources.title: Runway Gen-4 References
claims: Search summary: references are used as image_1 to image_3, up to three; a clear face and costume in a simple setting gives steadier results than cluttered lifestyle references.

sources.title: Seedream 4.0 (Freepik docs)
claims: Search summary: Seedream 4.0 takes up to 6 reference images (3.0 took 4) and keeps character identity and lighting better across batch outputs.
sources.notes: No ByteDance primary page was reached.

sources.title: Pika Scene Ingredients guide
claims: Search summary: Scene Ingredients combines your own images (reported up to six); advice is a clean well-lit reference, a prompt that spends more words on the character than the background, and 4 to 6 second clips.

sources.title: How do I maintain character consistency in Dream Machine
claims: Search summary: 1080p can give better results with Character Reference; tag the main character with @character in a normal prompt.
sources.notes: The page returned 404 when fetched.

sources.title: Midjourney expands image control with Omni Reference
claims: Search summary: reports the --ow range and that Midjourney advises not going above medium values such as 400 without need because quality can degrade.

sources.title: Reference images keep faces consistent but ignore character size/scale
claims: A user composing character references into a scene wanted a 1.4x height ratio; every render came near 1.1x, across about 15 phrasings and even a two-figure reference with the true ratio.
A text-only prompt with no references gave 1.4x at the first try, so the model re-derives size when it composes references.

A reply suggests limiting references to face and clothing, describing height by body alignment (where one head reaches on the other) and fixing scale first, then applying references in an edit turn; not confirmed by the poster.
sources.notes: Single user report, replies unconfirmed.

sources.title: Scaling Consistency: Predictable Subject Size Across Angles
claims: Vendor heuristics, not measured: reference at 35-50 mm look, subject inside the central 60% of the frame, one 4-6 s clip per angle anchored to the same still.
Remove subject descriptors from the motion prompt and use damping words (subtle, slow, steady); a subject that grows during camera motion means the move is too aggressive.
sources.notes: Marketing article; its own sample prompt contradicts its advice to leave out subject descriptors.

sources.title: Insert Anything: Image Insertion via In-Context Editing in DiT
claims: One model inserts a person, object or garment from a reference into a target scene, mask-guided or text-guided, keeping identity and fine detail while adapting colour and texture to the scene.

sources.title: Nano Banana Pro image generation in Gemini: Prompt tips
claims: Say what must stay the same ('keeping everything else the same'), give each reference image a role, and name the canvas and framing in the prompt (9:16, 21:9, wide shot).
Nothing on size or scale of subjects; complex blends and lighting changes can add artifacts.
sources.notes: Date approximate: the page was read without a date; check before citing.

sources.title: Kling AI Camera Control: Master Push, Pull, Pan & Tilt in AI Video
claims: Vocabulary that Kling responds to: push in, pull back, pan left/right, tilt up/down, track forward, orbit slowly, static camera.
Give each shot one main camera action; stacking push, pan, tilt and zoom can make results unstable.
Do not pair contradictory instructions such as a static camera with an orbit.
Name a slow or steady speed; a note discouraging sudden motion can reduce erratic movement.
Pull-backs need a clear subject and an environment to reveal; pans confuse when the subject moves fast the other way; push-ins on fast subjects are hard to control.
sources.notes: Vendor blog; results are probabilistic per the page.

sources.title: Runway Gen-4.5: directing motion (image-to-video)
claims: For image-to-video describe change over time, not what the image already shows.
Direct subject and camera separately; if one should stay still, say so, otherwise the model tends to move both.
Most reliable move names: push-in, pull-back, pan, tilt, dolly, orbit, crane.
Add a pacing word (slow, gradual, subtle, rapid, continuous) or the move comes out generic.
Motion the frame cannot support (unseen body parts, contradicting the image state) is ignored or degraded. Durations offered: 5, 8 or 10 s.
sources.notes: API aggregator documenting Runway Gen-4.5; not Runway itself.

sources.title: Kling AI Camera Movement Prompts: A Director's Complete Reference
claims: Covers locked-off, push-in, pull-out, dolly, tracking, tilt, pan, handheld drift, crane, aerial and orbit with example wording.
Moves are set to about 5 s of travel; pans stay under roughly 30 to 45 degrees and orbits around 30 degrees per clip, never above 45.
Failure modes: two moves in one prompt, fast moves (warping), very wide or 360-degree orbits, dollies without foreground/midground/background depth (they read as zooms).
Claims 79% usable camera moves when five common mistakes are avoided versus 34% otherwise; this is the site's own unreplicated figure.
sources.notes: Numbers are the author's own testing; treat as a rule of thumb.

sources.title: 100 cinematic camera prompts you can copy
claims: Always include a speed word (slow, creeping, fast); the same orbit reads romantic when slow and frantic when fast.
Use one camera move per shot, two at most; three or more confuses the model.
A two-move combo works when one move leads into the other with a clear trigger moment.
Smooth predictable moves such as crane and aerial suit AI models; speed ramps work when the prompt names the moment the speed changes.
sources.notes: Model rankings in the page are the author's opinion.

sources.title: Runway Gen-4 guide: 5/10-second image-to-video prompts
claims: Write subject motion, camera motion, scene response and motion style, in that order; keep to one subject action and one camera move.
Treat each 5 or 10 s generation as one shot; combining a transformation, an orbit and a scene change makes motion compete.
Avoid negative instructions and do not list every visible object.
Cropping the source image to another aspect ratio can remove details before motion is made; fix composition in the image first.
When motion is wrong, simplify the prompt before changing the image; change one variable at a time.

sources.title: Runway Gen-4 Turbo prompts
claims: To keep the camera still, state it positively, for example "Camera holds completely static".
Negative phrasing is not supported and describing an absence of movement can produce movement.
One scene and one primary action per generation; sequential actions or scene changes give inconsistent results.
Use 5 s for single actions and reveals, 10 s for longer or atmospheric shifts; lead with action verbs and pacing words.

sources.title: The Ultimate Veo 3.1 Prompt Guide
claims: Write prompts like a shot list: subject and action, style, camera work, lighting and atmosphere, setting, technical specs.
Camera moves to request: slow pan, dolly-in, tracking, handheld, crane, whip-pan; shot types: establishing wide, push-in reveal, reaction, payoff, POV.
Name a lighting style (low-key, high-key, noir, motivated, backlight, haze) instead of "cinematic".
Clips are 4, 6 or 8 s; longer pieces are assembled from several clips in an editor like Flow.
Overloaded prompts and many characters are weak spots; start with one main character.
sources.notes: The page contradicts itself on maximum length; the 4/6/8 s figure is the technical note.

sources.title: How to Write Prompts That Work for Sora 2
claims: Open with camera angle and movement (low-angle tracking, descending overhead drone); say so if the camera should stay still because the model drifts subtly by default.
Describe light source and quality (side light with strong shadows, soft diffuse from above); specific stock or camera references beat the word "cinematic".
Keep clips roughly 5 to 10 s; consistency drifts longer, so edit short segments together.
Use precise verbs (sprinting, strolling) not "moving"; gentle motion like a scarf in a breeze beats storms and liquid collisions.

sources.title: Sora 2 Prompting Guide (OpenAI Cookbook)
claims: Use one camera setup and one clear camera move per shot; one clear subject action per shot, written as small countable beats.
Shorter clips follow instructions more reliably; two 4 s clips stitched in editing may beat one 8 s clip.
Describe light quality and direction, name 3 to 5 palette colours and repeat them across shots.
Multi-shot prompts are possible if each shot block has its own camera, action and lighting; or generate shots standalone and edit.
Reuse identical wording for characters, wardrobe and lighting across shots; an image can anchor the first frame.
sources.notes: Sora availability is reported as ending in 2026; the guidance still applies to other models in spirit.

sources.title: AI video keeps adding cuts: a troubleshooting guide to one continuous shot
claims: Cuts appear when a prompt describes several moments; words such as "then", "cut to" and "reveals" signal a new beat or viewpoint.
Limit the prompt to one location, one main subject and one visible action; remove sequence and transition language.
State the camera plan separately: fixed shot, simple track or slow push-in, not several moves.
A cue like "one continuous shot from a fixed medium-wide camera angle" helps but does not guarantee the result.
Test one change at a time and log where the cut occurs.
sources.notes: Redirected from veo3gen.app. No controlled tests.

sources.title: What is the cut-hide technique in AI filmmaking?
claims: Separately generated clips rarely match exactly in light, background and colour; hide the seam by cutting during strong motion.
A still frame between two moving segments is the hardest place to hide a cut; cut on action.
Put strong foreground action opposite the seam region; correct the small colour gap with a slight curve adjustment.
With extension overlap, start the pick-up at about the third frame because the first frames often contain errors.
sources.notes: Vendor FAQ promoting its agent.

sources.title: How do you maintain consistent lighting across multiple AI video shots?
claims: Set lighting rules once per project (sources, shadow colour, contrast) in a style document rather than per clip.
Keep a fixed lighting slot in every prompt and describe the light source concretely; colour-temperature drift is the commonest inconsistency.
Repeat one locked style block at the start of every prompt.
Chain clips by carrying the last seconds of one into the next, described as stronger than single-frame methods; apply one unified grade in post.
sources.notes: Vendor FAQ.

sources.title: Every AI-generated shot invents its own light: how to keep lighting consistent
claims: Each clip is a stateless generation, so the model re-decides light direction, colour and quality every time; small rewordings cause visible change.
Define the light source in one sentence and reuse the exact wording in every shot of the scene; give colour temperature in Kelvin where accepted.
Light the widest shot first, then use that approved frame as a reference for closer shots.
Keep key-light direction consistent across angles and record source, direction, temperature in the scene plan.
Regenerating from a locked reference frame beats rewriting the prompt; check colour on full-size frames.

sources.title: AI Video Lighting Prompts: Volumetric Light & Golden Hour
claims: Name source, direction, intensity and colour rather than vague words like "warm".
Reference colour temperatures: golden hour about 3000 to 3500 K, midday 5500 to 6500 K, tungsten about 3200 K; long shadows anchor time of day.
Atmosphere (haze, fog, dust) makes light beams visible; match light to material (soft for skin, hard for metal, backlight for glass).
In multi-shot scenes repeat the shared light source, mood and shadow direction in each shot.
Phrase guardrails positively (steady light, controlled highlights) instead of listing problems.
sources.notes: Kelvin figures are conventional photography values, not model specs.

sources.title: How to write AI video prompts
claims: Six-part prompt: subject, action, setting, camera movement, lighting, style.
Use only one camera move per clip; for complex movement generate separate shots and cut them together.
If movement is unpredictable, lock the camera as static; give the feel and duration of a move, such as a slow steady push-in.
Name the light source and quality (soft window light from one side, warm tone); avoid "good lighting".

sources.title: Where Should Your Actor Look? Eyelines, Explained
claims: Keep the camera on one side of the line between two characters so each gaze points the same way from shot to shot.
Crossing the line reverses gaze directions and disorients the viewer.
If you must cross, use a neutral cutaway, or move the camera continuously across the line.
Use an establishing shot for group scenes and two- or three-shots to keep eyelines clear; map the lines while storyboarding.
Match eyeline height; looking down suggests authority, looking up vulnerability.
sources.notes: Film-school source, not about AI.

sources.title: What is the 180-degree rule in film?
claims: The camera stays on one side of the imaginary line so each subject keeps the same left/right position.
Screen direction must carry across cuts: a car moving right to left should keep doing so in the next shot.
Crossing the line is a deliberate tool for unease; bend it with a neutral shot on the line, a visible camera move across it, or a cutaway.
sources.notes: Film-school source, not about AI.

sources.title: Axis of Action (180-Degree Rule)
claims: The axis of action runs between two characters or along a subject's movement; the 180-degree rule keeps the camera on one side.
Filmmakers break it deliberately for horror, a shift of viewpoint, or to cheat the line in ensembles.
Crossing without a reason can make a moving subject seem to reverse direction.
sources.notes: Short dictionary entry.

sources.title: Multi-scene AI video
claims: Plan the sequence first: storyboard, style guide with reference images and a shot plan with framing, movement and duration per scene.
Draw still frames of key moments first because fixing drift in a still is faster than in video.
Prompt template: fixed opening (style, mood), changing middle (the action), fixed closing (lighting, camera, format).
The strongest continuity method is using the last frame of one scene as the start image of the next.
Trim first and last frames to remove artifacts and grade to a common look; a transition fixes a bad edit point, regeneration fixes a bad scene.

sources.title: Multi-shot AI video generator
claims: Single-shot tools make one continuous take; multi-shot output is several connected shots and needs a plan of how they relate.
Use a logical size progression (wide, medium, close-up, detail, back to wide); random angle jumps feel disjointed.
Give each shot the same fields: subject, action, location, camera, lighting, style, duration; one primary action each.
Keep sequences short because more cuts give more chances for continuity to break; carry the last frame forward.

sources.title: How to create multi-cut cinematic AI videos
claims: A tool generates 3 to 5 shots for a 10 to 20 s video after writing a shot plan with camera positions, shot types and lighting notes.
Alternate wide shots (place) and close-ups (detail or emotion); follow shots track the subject.
Reviewing and editing the plan before generating is the cheap place to fix order, angles and lighting.
sources.notes: Vendor tutorial for its own product.

sources.title: Which AI video shot types fail most often?
claims: Multi-character contact shots, POV shots and over-the-shoulder shots are weak spots; reword rarely helps, change references or model.
Continuous one-take shots lose character, location and camera continuity at each segment boundary.
Dense fast-cut scenes overload the model; split them in two.
Plan about three generations per usable result.
sources.notes: Vendor FAQ; model-specific.

sources.title: Why is cutting on a still frame between AI-generated clips a problem?
claims: Cutting on a still frame exposes the seam because the eye scans a static image and finds small colour or lighting differences.
Choose edit points where both clips share movement.
Extension overlaps have bad first frames; usable action starts around frame three.
If a hold is needed, add a gentle camera move so motion carries the viewer across the join.
sources.notes: Vendor FAQ.

sources.title: What is an establishing shot?
claims: An establishing shot opens a scene and shows where it takes place and how people relate to the surroundings.
Usually a wide or aerial view, it also sets tone and can signal time passing.
Start wide to set geography before moving closer; reuse the same location framing across scenes to show time passing.
sources.notes: Film-school source.

sources.title: Shot reverse shot
claims: Shot reverse shot puts the camera on one subject and then on the reverse view; common in dialogue, often over-the-shoulder.
By default match focal length, depth of field, camera movement and shot size across both setups; vary them only for meaning.
There is no single correct coverage; more setups give editing options.
sources.notes: Film-school source.

sources.title: Types of camera shot sizes in film
claims: Sizes from extreme wide (subject small, place emphasised) through full, medium wide (knees up), cowboy, medium (waist up), medium close-up (chest up), close-up, to extreme close-up.
Wide shots convey isolation or grandeur; close-ups reveal emotion; a medium shot works as a buffer before an emotional close-up.
Changing shot size creates contrast that signals a shift to the viewer.
sources.notes: Film-school source.

sources.title: Match cuts and types of cuts
claims: Match cuts join two scenes through a shared element: graphic match (shape, colour, composition), match on action, sound bridge, repeat cut.
Match on action carries a movement across two shots and gives momentum.
J-cuts and L-cuts overlap audio from one scene with the picture of the next.
sources.notes: Film-school source.

sources.title: What cinematic vocabulary terms improve AI video prompts?
claims: Name shot size, angle and movement first; then focal length, depth of field and exact aspect ratio.
Describe light by source, direction and contrast, not "warm"; replace "cinematic", "beautiful" with specific terms.
Recommends stating what must not appear because models drift to defaults (conflicts with Runway-style positive-only advice).
No benchmarks back the ranking of terms; examples are single productions.
sources.notes: Promotional page.

sources.title: Cinematic AI video prompts
claims: Push-in gives emotional emphasis, tracking gives momentum, handheld gives organic feel, orbit suits product reveals.
Low angle suggests authority, high angle vulnerability, tilted angle tension.
Sample prompts pair a move with a lens look, for example a slow push-in with shallow depth of field and an 85 mm lens look.
Change one element at a time and keep approved ones.
sources.notes: Page does not cover clip duration.

sources.title: The aspect ratio mistake that wastes 68% of your AI-generated video
claims: Cropping 16:9 (1920x1080) to 9:16 (608x1080) discards about 68% of horizontal pixels.
Match the reference image to the target ratio; a square image in a 16:9 tool makes the model invent edges.
Choose the final platform first and keep one ratio per sequence; generate natively for each platform.
Veo 3.1 reportedly supports native 9:16 output.
sources.notes: Pixel arithmetic is checkable; the rest is the author's experience.

sources.title: How does an editor control the rhythm of a film?
claims: Average shot length sets the audience baseline; many modern films sit around 4 to 6 s per shot.
Shorter shots raise tension, longer shots give calm; deviation from the baseline shapes mood.
Time cuts to emotional beats, even holding longer than seems necessary; long takes stay engaging through composition and movement.
sources.notes: Film-school source.

sources.title: Furious film editing: five films that average 2 seconds per shot
claims: Five films with about 2 s average shots and roughly 3000 shots each were played at 12x; only Mad Max: Fury Road stayed easy to follow.
Clear framing (viewer need not hunt for where to look) makes fast cutting readable; pointless fast cutting pulls viewers out.
sources.notes: Experiment by editor Vashi Nedomansky.

sources.title: How to create one-shot continuous videos with Seedance 2.0
claims: Plan the camera route (start, path, end) and the transition point for each change of scene, such as a doorway, corner, fog or focus shift.
Write the journey chronologically and state explicitly that the take has no cuts.
Physical transitions (doorways, curtains, stairs, fog) work more reliably than one environment morphing into another.
One generation runs up to 15 s; extensions add about 4 to 15 s; each extension prompt should restate the continuity.
sources.notes: Vendor tutorial.

sources.title: Wan 2.2 Prompting Guide: image-to-video in 4 steps
claims: Image-to-video prompt: main movement, camera behaviour, lighting or weather, and speed or strength of motion.
Describe motion not appearance; animate only elements visible in the image.
Use concrete camera verbs (pans, zooms, sways, slow push-in, orbit); for a static camera say so explicitly.
sources.notes: Does not address clip length.

sources.title: How to avoid continuity errors in AI-generated videos
claims: Error types: identity, wardrobe/props, environment, lighting/colour, screen direction, temporal shimmer, camera perspective.
Storyboard first and last frame of each shot so they connect; map screen direction and lighting per shot; chain from the previous final frame.
For a big lighting jump (bright exterior to dark interior) generate an intermediate bridging clip.
Hide seams with cutaways, close-ups or environment shots; keep clips short and prompts templated.

sources.title: How do I create static camera shots in Dream Machine?
claims: Ray2 drifts the camera slightly by default.
Opening the prompt with "still camera shot of" or "locked viewpoint of" is reported to keep the camera fixed.
sources.notes: Page returned 404 to fetch; claims from search result text only.

sources.title: How to Stop Unwanted Camera Motion in AI Prompts
claims: Recommends 'Static camera, locked shot' once; stacking 'stable', 'still', 'smooth' dilutes it. Keep prompts under 15 words with at most 2-3 motion keywords.
Claims a still source image cuts unwanted motion by 60-70% (internal numbers, not shared) and that drift sets in around 3.5 s, so keep the middle of a short clip.
Mechanical terms (tripod, locked-off) hold better than handheld, which adds randomness.
sources.notes: Vendor claims without data.

sources.title: Stop unwanted camera movement in AI video
claims: Put a positive lock block first ('locked eye-level medium shot from one fixed tripod position'), then an exclusion list (zoom, push-in, pan, tilt, orbit, dolly, drift, reframing).
Write invariants: subject size stays constant, side seams and floor line stay put; leave about 10% padding around the widest movement; keep a walking subject free to leave the frame.
Diagnose by comparing first, middle, last frames: a subject that grows while the edges move out is a zoom; edges sliding together is a pan; bent lines with fixed anchors is background warp.
sources.notes: Single practitioner article, no measurements.

sources.title: Firefly image to video keeps adding a slight push-in or pan
claims: A user reports that with every model in Firefly, the clip still gets a slight push-in or pan despite prompts forbidding zoom, pan, tilt and dolly, and asks for a true locked-camera mode.
A community expert's reply: negative prompts often do the opposite; state positively that the camera is fixed.
sources.notes: One thread, 20 views when read.

sources.title: Image-to-video that actually moves, not just wiggles
claims: Too little motion: write a change (start state to end state, then hold), use committed verbs (open, turn, lift), drop 'subtly move', 'gently animate', 'drift', which give a wiggle; one action per shot.

Locked camera: state 'locked tripod shot (no camera movement)', give the primary motion to the subject, say the background stays static, avoid handheld words; orbit about 10 degrees keeps a subject centred.
sources.notes: Original URL on veo3gen.app redirects here. Practitioner advice, untested claims.

sources.title: Photo to video tips
claims: Name a static setup ('static shot', 'locked camera') even to keep the composition, because without it the model may add drift; a locked shot means the camera stays fixed and only subjects move.
One primary movement per clip, 5-10 s, prompts of 20-40 words; no numeric drift tolerance is given.

sources.title: Improving Video Generation with Human Feedback (VideoAlign / VideoReward)
claims: Builds a large human preference dataset for video with pairwise labels on several dimensions, and a multi-dimensional reward model, VideoReward.
Reports VideoReward beating earlier reward models, and Flow-DPO beating Flow-RWR and plain fine-tuning.
Flow-NRG lets the user weight several objectives at inference time.
sources.notes: Abstract only; numbers are in the full paper (search summary says 182k labelled examples, three axes: visual quality, motion quality, text alignment).

sources.title: VisionReward: Fine-Grained Multi-Dimensional Human Preference Learning for Image and Video Generation
claims: Scores a picture or clip with a hierarchy of yes/no visual questions combined by linear weights, so the score can be explained.
Reports 17.2% better preference prediction than VideoScore.
Text-to-video models tuned with it win 31.6% more pairwise comparisons than ones tuned with VideoScore.

sources.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
claims: Names position bias, verbosity bias and self-enhancement bias in LLM judges, plus weak reasoning.
A strong judge (GPT-4) agreed with human preferences over 80% of the time, as often as humans agree with each other.
sources.notes: Text judges, not vision; the biases are the reason to randomise order and use a different judge from the generator.

sources.title: Vision language models are blind
claims: Seven very simple visual tasks (count circles in a logo, count line crossings, do two circles touch) get only 58.07% average accuracy from four top VLMs.
The best model scored 77.84%; humans would be near 100%.
Accuracy falls when shapes overlap or sit close together and rises when they are well separated.
Probing suggests the vision encoder holds the information but the language side fails to use it.

sources.title: Evaluating Text-to-Visual Generation with Image-to-Text Generation (VQAScore, GenAI-Bench)
claims: Asking a VQA model whether the picture shows the prompt and reading the probability of yes (VQAScore) beats CLIPScore on compositional prompts.
CLIPScore acts like a bag of words and cannot tell reversed meanings apart.
GenAI-Bench has 1,600 compositional prompts and over 15,000 human ratings; VQAScore also extends to video.

sources.title: Video-T1: Test-Time Scaling for Video Generation
claims: More test-time compute (more noise candidates scored by a verifier) steadily improved video quality on text-to-video benchmarks.
Tree-of-Frames grows and prunes video branches frame group by group, which is cheaper than scoring whole videos.
sources.notes: No numbers in the abstract.

sources.title: VISTA: a test-time self-improving video generation agent
claims: Splits the idea into a temporal plan, makes several videos, picks one by pairwise tournament, then three critic agents (visual, audio, context) feed a reasoning agent that rewrites the prompt.
Reports up to a 60% pairwise win rate over strong baselines; humans preferred it in 66.4% of comparisons.
Tested on single-scene and multi-scene generation.

sources.title: FilmAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for End-to-End Film Automation in Virtual 3D Spaces
claims: Agents play director, screenwriter, actor and cinematographer, with iterative feedback and revision to check scripts and reduce hallucination.
Human raters scored it 3.98 of 5 over 15 ideas; with GPT-4o it still beat a single-agent o1.
Runs in a 3D virtual space, not on a video model.

sources.title: VPO: Aligning Text-to-Video Generation Models with Prompt Optimization
claims: Rewrites short user prompts under three principles: harmless, accurate, helpful.
Notes that plain LLM rewriting can distort intent, drop key details or add safety risk, and ignores the resulting video.
Trains with feedback on both the text and the generated video; reports better safety, alignment and quality across several video models.

sources.title: Prompt-A-Video: Prompt Your Video Diffusion Model via Preference-Aligned LLM
claims: Rewrites user prompts for one specific video model, noting generic rewriters ignore which model will run the prompt.
Builds the rewriter by reward-guided prompt evolution, fine-tuning, then DPO on multi-dimensional rewards.
sources.notes: No numbers in the abstract.

sources.title: VideoRepair: Improving Text-to-Video Generation via Misalignment Evaluation and Localized Refinement
claims: A multimodal LLM asks generated questions about the video to find which regions are wrong; the correct parts are kept.
Only the flawed regions are regenerated with a new prompt and blended back; training-free and model-agnostic.
Beat baselines on EvalCrafter and T2V-CompBench with four video backbones.

sources.title: OR-Bench: An Over-Refusal Benchmark for Large Language Models
claims: 80,000 harmless-but-borderline prompts in 10 categories, with about 1,000 hard ones, plus 600 toxic prompts as a control.
Across 32 models from 8 families, safer alignment tends to come with more refusals of harmless prompts.
sources.notes: Text models, but the same trade-off is reported by users of video filters.

sources.title: Improving Text-to-Image Consistency via Automatic Prompt Optimization (OPT2I)
claims: An LLM rewrites the prompt over several rounds using a consistency score of the last image, with no model tuning.
Raised the DSG consistency score by up to 24.9% on MSCOCO and PartiPrompts while FID stayed stable.

sources.title: DirecT2V: Large Language Models are Frame-Level Directors for Zero-Shot Text-to-Video Generation
claims: An instruction-tuned LLM acts as director and writes a separate prompt per frame group so one abstract prompt can tell a changing story.
Zero-shot; needs no training; shows story-like coherence qualitatively, no numbers in the abstract.

sources.title: VideoScore2: Think before You Score in Generative Video Evaluation
claims: Scores visual quality, text-to-video alignment and physical or common-sense consistency, and writes its reasoning.
Trained on 27,168 human-labelled videos (supervised then GRPO); 44.35 accuracy in-domain and 50.37 average out-of-domain.
Shown to help as a reward in best-of-N sampling.
sources.notes: Accuracy figures are low in absolute terms: even the best judge is often wrong. Spot check 2026-11-08: the in-domain 44.35 point-score accuracy matches the abstract; the out-of-domain 50.37 average was not confirmed.

sources.title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
claims: Without outside feedback, models asked to revise their own answers often do not improve and sometimes get worse.
Argues a loop needs an external signal (a tool, a reference, a different check) to help.
sources.notes: Reasoning tasks, not video; relevant to critic loops that only reuse the generator.

sources.title: LLM-grounded Video Diffusion Models
claims: An LLM first writes dynamic scene layouts from the prompt, and these steer the video model, with no extra training.
Beat the base video model on requested attributes and motion patterns.

sources.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
claims: Sampling many answers and taking the one most of them agree on beat a single greedy answer on reasoning tasks (gains of 3.9 to 17.9 points).
sources.notes: Text reasoning; the idea of asking a judge twice is borrowed from it.

sources.title: Davidsonian Scene Graph: Improving Reliability in Fine-grained Evaluation for Text-to-Image Generation
claims: Question-and-answer scoring of a picture goes wrong when generated questions hallucinate, repeat or omit parts of the prompt.
The VQA model can also contradict itself (deny an object, then describe its colour); atomic questions in a dependency graph fix much of this.
Releases DSG-1k, 1,060 prompts.

sources.title: MLLM-as-a-Judge: Assessing Multimodal LLM-as-a-Judge with Vision-Language Benchmark
claims: Multimodal models judge well when comparing two items, but scoring one item and ranking a batch diverge strongly from human preference.
Even GPT-4V showed bias, hallucination and inconsistent verdicts; the authors call these judges not yet fully reliable.

sources.title: Disclosing use of altered or synthetic content
claims: Realistic altered or synthetic content must be disclosed at upload via the "AI use" setting, including a real person made to say or do something they did not.
Clearly unrealistic content (fantasy, fully animated) and minor aesthetic edits, AI help with scripts, captions, or upscaling need no disclosure.
The label may show on the player (photoreal, music) or in the expanded description; repeated non-disclosure can bring removal or loss of Partner Program access.

sources.title: Meta's approach to labeling AI-generated content and manipulated media
claims: "AI info" labels come from industry-shared signals in the file or from the uploader's own disclosure.
AI content is removed only if it breaks other policies; fact-checker ratings of "False" or "Altered" cut distribution.
Higher-risk deceptive content can get a more prominent label.
sources.notes: The page does not mention C2PA or IPTC by name.

sources.title: C2PA Technical Specification 2.1
claims: A Content Credential is a signed manifest of assertions (edit actions, device, thumbnail, content bindings).
Manifests can be stripped from a file; soft bindings such as fingerprints or invisible watermarks let a copy be matched back to a stored manifest.
Validation shows the record is well formed and signed, not that the content is good or true.
sources.notes: Read the first 100,000 of about 519,000 characters.

sources.title: SynthID
claims: Invisible watermark added at creation to images and video; claimed to survive cropping, filters, frame-rate change and lossy compression.
A detector portal checks files from Google and named partners; it only finds SynthID marks.
No accuracy or false-positive figures are published on the page.

sources.title: EU AI Act, Article 50: transparency obligations
sources.publisher: Future of Life Institute (text of the Act)
claims: From 2 August 2026, providers must make generated video and audio detectable as artificial in a machine-readable way.
Deployers must disclose deepfakes; for evidently artistic, creative or fictional work the disclosure may be limited to a notice that does not hamper showing it.
sources.notes: Summary of the page, not legal advice.

sources.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability
claims: Concludes that, with today's technology, prompts alone do not give enough human control for the user to be the author of the output.
Human expression visible in the output, creative selection and arrangement, and creative modification of outputs can be protected.
Repeated re-prompting until an output is acceptable does not by itself create authorship.
sources.notes: Read by text extraction; located the key conclusions, not every section.

sources.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence (hub page)
claims: Part 2 (copyrightability) was published 29 January 2025; Part 3 (generative AI training) as a pre-publication version on 9 May 2025.
Lists registration decisions on AI-assisted works, including Zarya of the Dawn.
sources.notes: Only the hub page was read for Part 3, not the report itself.

sources.title: Responsible AI and usage guidelines for Veo
claims: Prompts and outputs are checked for categories such as violence, sexual, derogatory and toxic content; a blocked output may carry a numeric support code naming the category (child, celebrity, violence, third-party content and others).
Requests depicting children are rejected unless personGeneration allows it, and photoreal prominent people unless the project is allow-listed.
If fewer videos return than asked, some were blocked; if a block looks wrong, the page says to send feedback.

sources.title: How to fix Veo 3's sensitive content warning
claims: Says the filters scan both the prompt and the generated pixels and are over-tuned, so harmless prompts get blocked.

Fixes: turn off prompt enhancement (it can add flagged words), cut the prompt down and add parts back one at a time, check start and end frames for logos or look-alike faces, swap trigger words ("shoot" for "capture").
sources.notes: One practitioner; the word swaps are not documented by Google.

sources.title: Sora 2 system card
claims: Downloads carry a visible moving watermark, and internal tools can identify Sora-made video and audio.
Likeness use goes through opt-in consent (cameos) with extra safeguards when real people appear; users who may be under 18 get stricter limits.
sources.notes: Page itself not opened; claims come from a search summary of it.

sources.title: OpenAI details Sora 2 safeguards for likeness, audio, and harmful content
claims: Reports that every Sora video carries visible and invisible provenance marks and embedded C2PA metadata.
Reports uploaders of photos of people must attest to consent, and images of children or young-looking people get tighter moderation.
sources.notes: Secondary report of an OpenAI note; no external evaluation data cited.

sources.title: Set your channel or video audience (made for kids)
claims: Creators must set whether each video is made for kids; a video-level setting overrides the channel setting.
Made-for-kids videos lose comments, notifications and personalised ads; wrong settings can bring FTC or YouTube action.
sources.notes: The page itself does not define made-for-kids or discuss animation.

sources.title: Complying with COPPA: frequently asked questions
claims: COPPA covers services directed to children under 13 that collect personal information, and general services that know they do.
Child-directed is judged on the whole picture: subject, visuals, animated characters, music, age of models, ads and audience data; animated characters are only one factor.
sources.notes: Read the first 100,000 of about 142,000 characters.

sources.title: Building effective agents
claims: An evaluator-optimizer loop (one call generates, another critiques) pays off when there are clear criteria and feedback measurably improves the result.
Agents should pause for human feedback at checkpoints or blockers and stop at a maximum number of iterations.

sources.title: Disney and Universal sue AI image company Midjourney
claims: Disney and Universal sued Midjourney in June 2025 over generated copies of Homer Simpson, Minions, Elsa, Darth Vader and Yoda, and over training on their works.
The complaint contrasts Midjourney with services that reject such prompts, and flags its coming video tool.
sources.notes: Details taken from search summaries of coverage; outcome unknown.

sources.title: SAM 2: Segment Anything in Images and Videos
claims: Promptable segmentation for video with a streaming memory; 3x fewer user interactions than earlier approaches on video and about 6x faster than SAM on images.

sources.title: SAMURAI: Adapting Segment Anything Model for Zero-Shot Visual Tracking with Motion-Aware Memory
claims: SAM 2 tracks poorly in crowded scenes and with fast or self-occluding objects, and its fixed memory window lets errors carry on; motion-aware memory selection adds 7.1% AUC on LaSOT_ext, zero-shot.

sources.title: SAM2Long: Enhancing SAM 2 for Long Video Segmentation with a Training-Free Memory Tree
claims: SAM 2 picks memory greedily, so one wrong or missed mask spreads to later frames; a tree search over several mask pathways gains 3.0 points on average, up to 5.3 J&F on SA-V and LVOS.

sources.title: SAM 3: Segment Anything with Concepts
