claims: Detects, segments and tracks all instances of a concept given as a short noun phrase or image exemplars, with persistent identities in video; doubles the accuracy of earlier systems on its SA-Co benchmark (author claim).
Prompts are short noun phrases, which fits our finding that a plain kind word works and a long description fails.

sources.title: Depth Anything V2
claims: Monocular depth with models from 25M to 1.3B parameters, over 10x faster than Stable Diffusion based depth models; metric-depth variants are fine-tuned separately.

sources.title: Do generative video models understand physical principles? (Physics-IQ)
sources.publisher: Motamed, Culp, Swersky, Jaini, Geirhos (Google DeepMind)
claims: Physics-IQ covers fluid dynamics, optics, solid mechanics, magnetism and thermodynamics.
Sora, Runway, Pika, Lumiere, SVD and VideoPoet were tested; physical understanding is called severely limited.
Physical understanding is reported as unrelated to visual realism: a model can look real and still be wrong.
sources.notes: Abstract page only; no per-model scores read.

sources.title: Physics-IQ project page
claims: Fluid dynamics tends to work better than solid mechanics in the tested models.
Five categories: solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, magnetism.
The leaderboard did not load when fetched, so no per-model numbers were obtained.

sources.title: Towards World Simulator: PhyGenBench
claims: PhyGenBench: 160 prompts, 27 physical laws, 4 physics domains, scored by the PhyGenEval pipeline.
Current text-to-video models often produce physically implausible video, especially in dynamic scenes.
Scaling the model or engineering the prompt does not fully fix physical errors.

sources.title: WorldModelBench: Judging Video Generation Models As World Models
claims: 67K human labels over 14 frontier models; adds instruction-following and physics-adherence dimensions.
Catches subtle faults such as an object changing size, which breaks mass conservation.
The abstract reports a fine-tuned 2B judge with 9.9% lower error than GPT-4o at predicting world-modelling violations (corrected from 8.6% after a spot check).
sources.notes: Number corrected on 2026-11-08 after a spot check against the paper abstract.

sources.title: How Far is Video Generation from World Model: A Physical Law Perspective
claims: In a 2D collision testbed, models do well in-distribution and fail out of distribution.
Models copy the nearest training example (case-based) instead of learning a rule.
When mimicking, they weigh color first, then size, velocity and shape.
Scaling alone did not uncover the physical laws.

sources.title: Cosmos World Foundation Model Platform for Physical AI
claims: Open-weight world foundation models plus a curation pipeline and tokenizers, aimed at simulating environments for physical AI.
Framed as a base to fine-tune into custom world models for a given setup.
sources.notes: Only the abstract was read; no physics scores.

sources.title: How to fix warped hands and faces in AI-generated video
claims: Keep one subject, one action and one camera move per prompt; closed fists, resting hands and hands holding objects render best.
Reliable coherence is cited as roughly 5 to 15 seconds for top models; generate short and cut.
A hand flickered between four and six fingers for eight frames and passed unnoticed in a preview; check at full resolution frame by frame.
Fix by masking the region and regenerating it; it often takes two or three attempts.

sources.title: AI video troubleshooting: fix the five common failures
claims: For warped hands ask for simple visible poses, frame hands out if they are not the focus, keep shots short.
Jitter comes from fast or vague motion: add pace words and say what stays still ("static subject, slow camera push in").
Overloaded prompts get details ignored: subject and action first, cut idle clauses, stubborn details get their own sentence.

sources.title: Prompt tips for realistic AI video
claims: Floaty motion appears when weight is unspecified: state weight and acceleration.
Describe liquids and gases in slow gentle terms (honey dripping slowly, steam rising gently).
Keep camera moves simple and slow; minimal motion avoids complex physics; slow motion at 0.5x to 0.75x can hide leftover artifacts.
Complex hand movements are named as a common failure point; generate 3 to 5 variations.
sources.notes: Vendor guide.

sources.title: Kling physics bugs and motion deformation: a checklist
claims: Bug classes: floating feet, hands passing into props, melting fingers and rims, wrong identity after an occlusion.
Fixes: one stable grip, one container with one liquid action, enlarge props whose label drifts, avoid critical text.
Prompt order: scene geometry, stable subjects, one action, contact response, one camera move, preservation constraints.
Test one primary action and one contact chain per take; split the shot otherwise.
sources.notes: Reseller blog; the author says the examples are illustrative, not a benchmark.

sources.title: AI video physics test (summary of a HumanSignal comparison)
claims: Seedance 2.5, Veo 3.1 and Kling 3.0 Pro all failed a pour of 60% of a pint into an empty glass, in different ways; the shared fault was volume transfer.
Kling looked most realistic yet ended with about two glasses of water.
A crude clay previs passed as a motion and camera reference helped; less detail worked better.
One team's saved examples, not a benchmark; the source company sells training data.
sources.notes: Second-hand report of the HumanSignal post.

sources.title: VideoScience-Bench: can video models simulate science?
claims: 200 experiments, 103 concepts, 14 topics; seven models scored on five criteria.
Models score well on coherence and immutability but poorly on whether the right phenomenon happens.
Sora-2 and Veo-3 were clearly ahead; still weak on multi-concept scenes.
Examples: spaghetti that should break in three pieces breaks in two; Veo-3 morphs impossibly; Kling invents batteries in a solution.

sources.title: Why does Sora struggle with object physics?
claims: Failures listed: glass fracture, food that does not shrink when eaten, liquid level that does not drop when drunk, honey moving like water.
Similar objects in a crowd merge, lose identity or appear and vanish.
Physics reportedly degrades over about 20 to 30 seconds; hand-object contact is imprecise.
sources.notes: FAQ-style explainer; the 20 to 30 second figure is not verified against OpenAI.

sources.title: Why AI video generators mess up hands and faces
claims: Hands are hard because of joints, overlap, foreshortening, object contact and fast or hidden motion.
If hands are not essential keep them relaxed, out of frame or partly hidden; when they matter give each hand one concrete pose.
One hand action per short clip, object clearly visible, camera steady; the main fix is reducing complexity, negative prompts are a backup.

sources.title: AI video hands and faces
claims: Training data for gripping, pointing or partly hidden hands is thinner than for faces, so hands fail first.
Describe start and end hand positions rather than the motion, and put the hand description first.
Supply a reference image of the exact hand position beside the character reference.
sources.notes: Vendor blog.

sources.title: Can You Count to Nine? T2VCountBench
claims: Text-to-video models almost always fail to produce a requested object count of nine or fewer.
Prompt refinement and splitting the task did not easily fix it.
High object fidelity does not mean the count is right.
sources.notes: A search summary reported that the best model (Pika 2.2) reached about 50%; not confirmed on the page read.

sources.title: PhysGen: Rigid-Body Physics-Grounded Image-to-Video Generation
claims: Takes one image plus a force or torque, simulates rigid-body motion, then renders with video diffusion.
More physically plausible and controllable than purely data-driven image-to-video in numbers and a user study (ECCV 2024).

sources.title: PhysDreamer: Physics-Based Interaction with 3D Objects via Video Generation
claims: Uses motion priors from video models to estimate material stiffness of static 3D objects, then simulates their response to forces.
Shown on elastic objects such as flowers and a telephone cord; realism judged in a user study.

sources.title: No, Sora has not learned physics
claims: Cited failures: people, animals and limbs appear and disappear; chairs levitate; people change size.
Anatomy faults: six fingers, three arms, odd gaits, ants with four legs.
Argument: Sora predicts how the world looks, not how it works; when physics conflicts with pixel continuity the pixels win.
sources.notes: Opinion piece, with examples from OpenAI's own demos.

sources.title: Why Sora 2 struggles with physics-accurate motion
claims: Fast moves (jumps, flips) distort joints and can add or detach limbs.
Objects can pass through each other or fail to bounce or deform on impact.
Over many frames objects can teleport, change size or vanish, worst with fast or crowded motion.

sources.title: When Numbers Speak: Aligning Textual Numerals and Visual Instances in Text-to-Video Diffusion (NUMINA)
claims: A training-free fix that finds count mismatches in attention and regenerates; counting accuracy up 7.4% (1.3B), 4.9% (5B), 5.5% (14B) on Wan2.1.
The authors say structural guidance complements seed search and prompt enhancement, so counting is still unsolved by prompts alone.

sources.title: Sora limitations and workarounds
claims: Complex scenes show gravity errors, odd glass and liquid behavior and distorted human motion; simplify to one main action.
Legible text is rare and warps between frames: add type in post or use distant stylized signage.
Hybrid production: mix generated shots with hand-animated or simulated segments.

sources.title: Vertex AI video generation prompt guide
claims: For a negative prompt, name the unwanted things as a list ("wall, frame") rather than writing "no walls" or "don't".
Break a prompt into subject, action, scene, camera, lens, style, time and audio; be specific (named breed, not "animal").
Gradual changes should be subtle for short clips.
sources.notes: The page defers physics, hands and text to a separate best-practices page that was not read.

sources.title: MirrorWorld: Taming Video Diffusion Models for Mirror Reflection Generation
claims: Video diffusion models often give mirrors the wrong content or layout because they lack a scene-to-mirror relation.
Fix proposed is video inpainting with semantic and geometric alignment; this is research, not a prompt tip.

sources.title: How to add text to AI-generated video without it looking broken
claims: Models make text-shaped marks that read from afar and dissolve up close.
Put informational text (titles, subtitles) in the editor; for in-world signs make the sign as a still at about 2K, verify it, then animate it.
Keep the camera slow near text; a blurred or angled sign can imply words without spelling them.

sources.title: AI video generates wrong text: the real fix
claims: Text is painted as texture, and a letter correct in one frame can change by a later one.
Angled signs fail more than frontal ones; short common words (STOP) succeed more often than phrases.
Generate a clean blank sign and overlay the text in post with motion tracking.
sources.notes: Reseller blog.

sources.title: Fixing diffusion models' limited understanding of mirrors and reflections
claims: Latent diffusion models struggle with accurate reflections; the weakness depends on training data coverage.
The MirrorFusion 2.0 work was preferred by 84% of users over its baseline; the author says results are far from perfect.
sources.notes: Image-model work, not video; use for the direction of the problem only.

sources.title: AI video generators: limitations in 2025
claims: Physics workaround: show a filled glass rather than a pour, keep clips under 3 to 4 seconds.
Hands: keep them out of frame, at rest or in pockets; use wide shots; generate 10 to 20 variations.
Recommended length per clip for 2024-era models ranged from 2 to 5 seconds, up to 10 to 15 for Sora.
Budget 3 to 5 hours of editing per finished minute.
sources.notes: Model figures are for 2024-era tools.

sources.title: Why AI videos look fake: 7 fixes
claims: Objects drift or vanish: name key objects, keep the object count low, lock the camera, keep clips to 3 to 5 seconds.
Floaty motion: describe weight and ground contact and slow the action.
Wrong hands: crop them out or use simple poses (fists, open palms); generate several takes.

sources.title: Video models are zero-shot learners and reasoners
claims: Veo 3 shows some understanding of physical properties and tool use without being trained for it.
Presented as a trend, not as reliable physics.
sources.notes: Abstract only.

sources.title: Motion Prompting: Controlling Video Generation with Motion Trajectories
claims: A model conditioned on sparse or dense point trajectories controls object and camera motion that text cannot specify.
Physically plausible behavior emerges in the interactions; CVPR 2025.

sources.title: Wan 2.2 prompt guide
claims: Missing motion cues lead to static or morphing scenes; give every moving element a direction and a speed.
Use negative prompts (extra limbs, duplicate subjects, flicker, warped objects) after seeing a problem, not by default.
Negative prompts are not a substitute for a good positive prompt; contradictory instructions give unpredictable results.
sources.notes: Vendor page.

sources.title: How to prompt with Runway Gen-4 image to video
claims: Negative prompts are said to be unsupported for Gen-4 and can backfire; state what should happen ("the camera stays still").
Do not describe what is already in the image; describe only the next action.
One clear physical action per prompt; add subject motion first, check, then add camera motion.
sources.notes: Third-party reading of a Runway guide.

sources.title: Gemini API video generation page (Veo shutdown notice, Gemini Omni Flash)
claims: The page says Veo 3.1 Preview models in the Gemini API were shut down on 22 October 2026 and points users to Gemini Omni Flash or GA models.
Gemini Omni Flash: 3 to 15 second videos, native audio, text/image/video input, character consistency from up to 6 reference images.
Omni Flash supports multi-turn conversational editing and extension through the Interactions API.
sources.notes: The page did not contain the Veo parameter list; use it only for lifecycle facts.

sources.title: Luma Dream Machine API: video generation
claims: Models ray-2 and ray-flash-2; resolutions listed 540p, 720p, 1080 and 4k; example duration 5s; loop flag; camera motion is written in the prompt.
Start frame (keyframes.frame0) and end frame (frame1) can be set separately or together, as image URLs on Luma's own CDN.
Extend forward from a completed generation (frame0) or in reverse (frame1); two generation ids give an interpolation between clips.
A concepts list (for example dolly_zoom) and a list of supported camera-motion strings are available from the API.

sources.title: Video generation with Sora (OpenAI API guide)
claims: The guide states the Sora 2 models and Videos API were shut down on 24 September 2026 with no one-to-one replacement.
Characters: a 2-4 second clip makes a reusable non-human subject; the character's name must appear in the prompt (the id alone is not enough); up to two per video.
Extensions add up to 20s each, up to six times, 120s total; edits replace remix and small single-change edits keep more fidelity.
Rejected: real people, input images with human faces, copyrighted characters and music; content must suit under-18 audiences.

sources.title: Wan2.2 README (official repository)
claims: Variants: T2V-A14B and I2V-A14B (480P/720P), TI2V-5B (720P at 24 fps, 1280x704), S2V-14B (audio driven), Animate-14B.
The repo recommends prompt extension (Qwen models via Dashscope or local) to add detail; image-to-video can run with an empty prompt when extension is on.
I2V and S2V keep the input image's aspect ratio; the size value only sets the output area.
A14B on one GPU needs about 80GB VRAM; TI2V-5B runs on a 24GB card such as an RTX 4090.

sources.title: LTX-Video README (v0.9.x, legacy)
claims: Write one flowing paragraph of chronological detail, start with the main action, stay within 200 words.
Width and height should be divisible by 32; frame counts of the form 8k+1 (for example 257), best below 257; works best under 720x1280.
Keyframes and video segments can be pinned at target frame numbers with per-item strength (default 1.0); image-to-video starts at frame 0.
Save the seed to recreate a look; guidance scale 3-3.5; the repo is no longer actively developed and points to newer LTX versions.

sources.title: HunyuanVideo README (official repository)
claims: Default 129 frames at 720x1280 or 1280x720 (also 540p sizes); peak GPU memory about 60GB at 720p, 45GB at 544x960.
A fine-tuned prompt-rewrite model has Normal mode (better intent) and Master mode (adds composition, lighting, camera detail but may drop semantic detail).
This README covers text-to-video only; image-to-video is a separate project, HunyuanVideo-I2V.

sources.title: Runway API: using the API
claims: API examples use model gen4.5 for image-to-video and text-to-video; text-only goes to /v1/text_to_video, image-to-video requires promptImage.
referenceImages is a list of uri plus optional tag, and a tag can be mentioned in the prompt with at-syntax (for example @EiffelTower).
Ratios in examples: 1280:720 for video; the page lists no seed or promptText limit.

sources.title: Kling 2.5 Video Prompt Guide
claims: Six-layer formula: subject and appearance, action with kinetic verbs, environment, camera, lighting/atmosphere, technical specs; suggested length 50-100 words.
Negative prompts target morphing, distorted hands, flicker, jitter and frozen motion; test with 5s clips before 10s.
Weak points listed: lip-sync and dialogue, stiff static people, identity drift when appearance is over-described, ungrounded objects.
sources.notes: Reseller blog; its speed and quality claims are unverified.

sources.title: Seedance 1.0: Exploring the Boundaries of Video Generation Models
claims: Jointly trained for text-to-video and image-to-video; the abstract claims native multi-shot generation with a consistent subject.
Abstract claims a 5 second 1080p clip in 41.4 seconds on an NVIDIA L20 and about 10x inference speedup from distillation.
The abstract gives no prompt formula.

sources.title: Moonvalley Marey video generation in ComfyUI
claims: The page says the Moonvalley API is no longer available and the nodes are deprecated.
Text-to-video and image-to-video take a positive and a negative prompt; training data is based on 1080p.
Video-to-video has control_type Motion Transfer or Pose Transfer, and the input video must be longer than the target (over 5s for 5s).

sources.title: Hailuo 02 guide (Magic Hour)
claims: Hailuo 02 launched with text-to-video and image-to-video; start-and-end-frame and end-frame-only controls were added later in MiniMax apps.
Clips: 768p at 6 or 10 seconds, 1080p at 6 seconds.
The article says Hailuo 02 is no longer MiniMax's flagship and drops earlier unsupported lip-sync claims; availability varies by provider.

sources.title: How to write better Hailuo 2.3 prompts
claims: Order prompts as a viewer sees them: camera, subject, one action as a sequence, setting and light; prompts are capped at 2,000 characters.
15 bracketed camera commands (Push in, Pan, Tracking shot, Static shot...): one bracket runs moves together (max three), separate brackets run in sequence.
The prompt optimizer is on by default; turn it off once the prompt has exact bracket commands or product/expression constraints.
Image-to-video: prompt the change, say what stays still; input under 20MB, short edge over 300px, ratio between 2:5 and 5:2; 6s suits one action and one camera move.
Avoid stacking emotions or stunts in one clip and avoid labels like she is sad; describe the performance change.

sources.title: FLUX.1 Kontext announcement
claims: Kontext takes text and images together and edits by plain-language instruction; it keeps a reference character or object consistent across scenes.
Edits can be chained step by step, but long multi-turn sessions can add visual artifacts that lower quality.
Name the specific element to change so the rest of the image is left alone; make changes incrementally.

sources.title: Wan: Open and Advanced Large-Scale Video Generative Models
claims: Two sizes, 1.3B (8.19 GB VRAM) and 14B; the authors claim the 14B beats open-source and some commercial models on their benchmarks.
Supports image-to-video, instruction-guided video editing and personalised video generation.

sources.title: Stable Video Diffusion img2vid-xt model card
claims: One conditioning image in; trained for 25 frames at 576x1024; clips of about 4 seconds or less.
The card says it cannot be controlled through text and cannot render legible text.
Known problems: little or no motion or only slow pans, faces and people may be wrong, lossy autoencoder.

sources.title: Seedream 4 Prompt Engineering: The Complete Practical Guide
claims: Layer subject/action, composition, lighting and lens, style, technical controls, negative prompts; examples are short comma-separated lists.
Upload references before writing the prompt, give each a role (character, style, palette, product), use clean well-lit references.
To fight identity drift: clear reference, lock the seed, reduce variation; lock seeds and keep composition terms steady across a series.
sources.notes: Hosting-provider blog, not ByteDance.

sources.title: Veo 3.1 developer guide: timestamp prompting, multi-shot, API
claims: Each call makes 4, 6 or 8 seconds at 1080p in 16:9 or 9:16; longer films are chained 8s clips.
Timestamp prompting ([00:00-00:02] style segments) directs several shots in one 8s call; keep subject and scene details repeated across segments.
First frame is followed closely, the last frame is only a guide; 4s clips hit the end frame more tightly than 8s clips; input images must match the aspect ratio.
Three reference images is the practical ceiling; one character plus one setting is usually enough; extreme close-up faces can show artifacts.
sources.notes: Single author, unverified against Google docs; the Veo 3.1 preview is now shut down per the Google page.

sources.title: Pika 2.2 on Imagine.art docs
claims: Pika 2.2: 5 or 10 second clips, 720p or 1080p, seven aspect ratios (16:9, 9:16, 1:1, 4:5, 5:4, 3:2, 2:3).
Pikaframes: upload first and last frame, choose a 5 or 10 second transition; the prompt is optional.
With frames supplied, write only motion style, pacing and atmosphere because the frames already set the visuals.
sources.notes: Reseller documentation.

sources.title: Text-to-video prompt guide: how to prompt with Kling
claims: Formula: subject and its movement, then scene details, optionally camera language, lighting and atmosphere.
Keep to 2-4 main ideas; too many ideas overwhelm the model.
Image-to-video start frame minimum 300x300 pixels; 1920x1080 or 1280x720 recommended.

sources.title: How to craft Wan 2.2 AI video prompts
claims: Formula: subject + scene + movement, extended with aesthetic control (light, shot, lens, camera) and stylization.
For image-to-video use movement plus camera movement; adding fixed lens keeps the shot steady.

sources.title: Runway Aleph: the essentials
claims: Aleph 2 edits existing footage: source video up to 30s and 16MB, prompt up to 1,000 characters, up to 5 keyframe images; output 1080p SDR.
Pair an action verb (add, remove, change, replace) with a target; keep one edit per prompt, chain edits; say what must stay the same.
Original Aleph (Gen-4) uses only the first 5 seconds and can deform characters on complex camera moves; Aleph 2 is not built for new camera angles.
sources.notes: Scenario relays Runway's information.

sources.title: Mochi 1 preview model card
claims: Initial release is 480p (848x480 in the API example), 30 fps export; the card gives no clip length.
Extreme motion can cause minor warping; it does poorly on animated content and is tuned to photorealistic styles.

sources.title: HunyuanVideo: A Systematic Framework For Large Video Generative Models
claims: Over 13B parameters, called the largest open-source video model at release; the authors report professional raters preferring it to Runway Gen-3 and Luma 1.6.

sources.title: Wan 2.2: the essentials
claims: Hosted Wan 2.2: text, image and last-frame conditioning; max 5 seconds; 480p or 720p (1280x720); 24 fps, 16 fps for drafts.
Aim for 80-120 words in shot order starting with what the camera first sees; avoid contradictory instructions.
A negative prompt is supported and a default one is applied; overloaded or conflicting prompts hurt results.

sources.title: Runway Gen4.5: the essentials
claims: Inputs: text prompt, optional first-frame image, aspect ratio, duration 2 to 10 seconds, seed field.
The first-frame image should match the chosen aspect ratio to avoid stretching or black bars.
Describe how things move, not only what is in the scene.

sources.title: LTX-2 prompt guide
claims: One flowing paragraph in present tense, joining actions with as/then/while; for image-to-video describe the source image exactly and build on it.
Name perspective, angle, movement, speed and lens; put sounds inside the scene prose.
Show emotion through actions and physical reactions, not labels; avoid flicker, moire and exposure shifts.
LTX-2 Fast and Pro were retired on that host; the technique carries to LTX 2.3.

sources.title: Runway 4.5 on Imagine.art docs
claims: Durations 5, 8 or 10 seconds at 24 fps; text-to-video and image-to-video.
Use exact camera language (slow dolly forward); for image-to-video describe what should change, not what is visible.

sources.title: Kling 2.5 Turbo prompting guide
claims: Use one hero subject and one main action, lighting from a named source, mood cues; name the camera move exactly (slow push-in, drone follow, lateral track).
For image-to-video say what moves, what stays fixed and how the camera behaves.
Pitfalls: vague camera notes, too many simultaneous actions, no lighting plan, no anchor props, style mismatch.
sources.notes: Promotional; no negative-prompt or weakness section.

sources.title: Gen-4 Video Prompting Guide (Runway Help Center)
claims: Per search results, Runway says the model reads what should happen rather than what to avoid, and negated phrasing can backfire.
Page not fetched (403); the summary came from a web search.

sources.title: Runway Aleph help article
claims: Per search results, Aleph handles at most 5 seconds per generation and uses the first 5 seconds by default (trim tool picks another segment).
Prompt advice: one verb that sets the scope of the change plus a description of the target; no strict rules.
sources.notes: Page returned 403 on fetch.

sources.title: LTX-2.5 prompt guide
claims: Per search results, LTX says the model responds best to cinematic single-subject scenes with clear camera language, consistent lighting and well-described audio.
sources.notes: Not fetched.

sources.title: Seedance 1.0 docs (Freepik)
claims: Per search results, the suggested structure is subject + movement + scene + camera/style + atmosphere.
Search results from several third parties agree on subject, action, environment, camera, style order; no ByteDance prompt guide was found.
sources.notes: Fetch returned 403.

sources.title: Which AI video tool gives real camera angle and lens control (Higgsfield)
claims: Per search results, Cinema Studio sets camera, lens, aperture, lighting and 30+ movement presets in a panel before generation, so the prompt only needs scene action.
Identity is attached with an @ element mention (Soul ID); other sources disagree on whether Cinema Studio 3.5 or 4.0 is current.
sources.notes: Vendor marketing; not fetched.

sources.title: Marey by Moonvalley review
claims: Per search results, Marey offers trajectory control (draw object paths) and keyframing with multiple reference images on a timeline.
The reviewer gave it 3.2/10 in their own tests.
sources.notes: Not fetched; one reviewer's opinion.

sources.title: Seedream 4.0 (Hedra listing)
claims: Per search results, Hedra says Seedream 4.0 blends up to 6 reference images while another host says up to 14; the figures conflict.
sources.notes: Not fetched; conflicting number, check BytePlus.

sources.title: Kling image to video guide
claims: Prompt as subject plus movement, list each subject's movement in order; the picture already sets the scene.
A description far from the image may cause a cut or transition; photos tend to give static clips and the model may pan across a painting-like picture. Clips are 5 or 10 s.
sources.notes: Camera and start/end frame guidance are on separate Kling pages not read here.

sources.title: Seedance 1.5 Pro image-to-video API
claims: camera_fixed (default false) is a request flag for locked-tripod shots; if the camera drifts, set it true and also describe a locked-off camera in the prompt.
last_image steers the final composition; choose an end frame with framing and lighting close to the first to reduce jumpy transitions. Duration 4-12 s; the 1.5 family is being retired.
sources.notes: Host documentation of ByteDance's model, not ByteDance's own page.

sources.title: ComfyUI-PainterI2V (repository summary)
claims: Targets the slow-motion look of 4-step LoRAs (lightx2v) in Wan image-to-video by scaling motion with a motion_amplitude parameter, recommended 1.0 to 1.5 (about 15-50% more motion); no benchmark is given.
sources.notes: Read through an aggregator page, not the repository.

sources.title: StreamingT2V: Consistent, Dynamic, and Extendable Long Video Generation from Text
claims: Typical text-to-video models make only 16 or 24 frames; naive extension causes hard cuts between chunks.
Targets 80, 240, 600, 1200 or more frames with smooth transitions.
Short-term attention conditions each chunk on the previous chunk; long-term module reuses features of the first chunk to hold appearance.
Reports that image-to-video models used autoregressively stall (little motion) while its method keeps motion high.
sources.notes: Abstract and arXiv metadata only; ablation numbers not read.

sources.title: Long Context Tuning for Video Generation
claims: Widens a single-shot model to attend over all shots of a scene, learning scene-level consistency from data.
Uses interleaved 3D position embeddings and an asynchronous noise strategy per shot; adds no parameters.
Supports joint multi-shot generation and shot-by-shot autoregressive extension (context-causal attention for efficiency).
Shows compositional generation and interactive shot extension; abstract gives no numeric results.

sources.title: Frame Context Packing and Drift Prevention in Next-Frame-Prediction Video Diffusion Models (FramePack)
claims: FramePack gives important frames longer context within a fixed context length, so memory does not grow with video length.
Frame importance is by time proximity, feature similarity or a hybrid; inference over thousands of frames is possible.
Proposes drift-prevention methods against error accumulation; ablations compare streaming and bidirectional generation.
sources.notes: Numbers from the paper body not read.

sources.title: Self Forcing: Bridging the Train-Test Gap in Autoregressive Video Diffusion
claims: Exposure bias: models trained on true context drift when they must continue from their own imperfect frames.
Trains on self-generated history with KV caching and a video-level loss; a rolling KV cache extends length at inference.
Reports real-time streaming on one GPU with quality matching or beating slower non-causal diffusion models.

sources.title: Connected Self Forcing: Beyond Local Learning in Video Autoregression
claims: Self Forcing detaches cached history, cutting gradient paths between chunks, which limits long-horizon quality.
Reconnecting gradients across chunks (with shortcut gradient replay for memory) improves long-horizon quality and temporal consistency.
Inference procedure is unchanged; abstract has no numbers.

sources.title: From Slow Bidirectional to Fast Autoregressive Video Diffusion Models (CausVid)
claims: Converts a bidirectional video diffusion transformer to a causal one and distills 50 steps down to 4.
Scores 84.27 on VBench-Long and runs at 9.4 FPS on one GPU with KV caching.
Supports zero-shot image-to-video, video-to-video and dynamic (changing) prompts during generation.

sources.title: MovieDreamer: Hierarchical Generation for Coherent Long Visual Sequence
claims: Autoregressive model plans global narrative as visual tokens; diffusion renders them to frames.
A multimodal script carries character and visual-style details to keep identity continuous across scenes.
Claims better visual and narrative quality and longer durations than prior methods; no numbers in the abstract.

sources.title: VideoGen-of-Thought: Step-by-step generating multi-shot video with minimal manual intervention
claims: Training-free: one sentence becomes shot descriptions, then cinematic specs across five domains with self-validation.
Identity-preserving portrait tokens keep a character consistent; boundary-aware resets smooth shot transitions.
Beats baselines by 20.4% in within-shot face consistency and 17.4% in style consistency; 10x fewer manual adjustments.
sources.notes: Same title as res-009; this is the first posting.

sources.title: VideoGen-of-Thought (revised posting): Step-by-step generating multi-shot video
claims: Same method as the Dec 2024 posting; resubmitted as a new paper by mistake according to its comment.
Reports 20.4% better within-shot face consistency, 17.4% better style consistency, and over 100% better cross-shot consistency.
Needs 10x fewer manual adjustments than baselines.

sources.title: Automated Movie Generation via Multi-Agent CoT Planning (MovieAgent)
claims: Input is a script and a character bank; output is multi-scene, multi-shot video with consistent characters, subtitles and audio.
LLM agents play director, screenwriter, storyboard artist and location manager in a hierarchical chain-of-thought plan.
Claims state of the art on script faithfulness, character consistency and narrative coherence; abstract gives no numbers.

sources.title: DreamFactory: Pioneering Multi-Scene Long Video Generation with a Multi-Agent Framework
claims: LLM multi-agent framework for long, multi-scene video that keeps style and characters consistent.
Uses chain-of-thought to handle model uncertainty and proposes new cross-scene consistency metrics.
Releases a dataset of over 150 human-rated multi-scene videos.

sources.title: Anim-Director: A Large Multimodal Model Powered Agent for Controllable Animation Video Generation
claims: Agent writes storyline and director script, then generates consistent setting and scene images, then animates them.
The agent judges the visual quality of its own outputs and keeps the best, with no manual step.

sources.title: VideoStudio: Generating Consistent-Content and Multi-Scene Videos
claims: An LLM turns a prompt into a multi-scene script, then reference images are generated for each recurring entity.
A diffusion model conditioned on those references keeps content consistent across scenes.
Claims better visual quality, content consistency and user preference than prior video models.

sources.title: Lumiere: A Space-Time Diffusion Model for Video Generation
claims: Generates the whole clip in one pass with a Space-Time U-Net, instead of distant keyframes then temporal super-resolution.
Samples at full frame rate and low resolution over several space-time scales; supports image-to-video and inpainting.
sources.notes: Single-pass design is the cited reason for global temporal consistency.

sources.title: MAGI-1: Autoregressive Video Generation at Scale
claims: Predicts fixed-length chunks of frames one after another, enabling streaming generation.
Peak inference cost stays constant regardless of video length.
Largest variant has 24B parameters and supports context up to 4 million tokens.

sources.title: SkyReels-V3 Technique Report
claims: One diffusion-transformer model covers reference-image-to-video, video extension and audio-driven talking avatars.
Reports results near leading closed-source systems; abstract has no numbers.

sources.title: Frequency-Step Cache: Separating Synchronization and Repair for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
claims: Training-free cache for autoregressive video diffusion that decides when to fully recompute using a drift risk signal.
On SkyReels-V2, 2.36x speedup at an SSIM gain of 0.019 and PSNR gain of 0.5 dB over MotionCache.
At matched speed, SSIM +0.031, PSNR +1.0 dB and LPIPS -0.024 versus MotionCache.

sources.title: StoryDiffusion: Consistent Self-Attention for Long-Range Image and Video Generation
claims: Consistent Self-Attention is zero-shot: it shares information across images of a batch in pretrained text-to-image models to keep characters alike.
A Semantic Motion Predictor estimates motion between two images in semantic space to make smoother transitions for long videos.
Generates consistent image sequences and videos from a text story.
sources.notes: Do not confuse with the UX storyboarding paper of the same name (arXiv 2407.07672).

sources.title: Identity-Preserving Text-to-Video Generation by Frequency Decomposition (ConsisID)
claims: Tuning-free DiT model keeping a person identity across the video from one face image.
Low-frequency global facial features go to shallow layers; high-frequency local detail goes into transformer blocks.
Hierarchical training adapts a pretrained video model to identity preservation.

sources.title: MoCA: Identity-Preserving Text-to-Video Generation via Mixture of Cross Attention
claims: Mixture-of-cross-attention layers plus a latent video perceptual loss improve temporal identity coherence.
Builds CelebIPVid, 10,000 high-resolution videos from 1,000 people.
Beats existing methods by over 5% on face similarity.

sources.title: Phantom: Subject-consistent video generation via cross-modal alignment
claims: Handles single and multiple reference subjects in one framework.
Trained on text-image-video triplets to stop image content leakage and multi-subject confusion.
Claims to beat closed-source commercial solutions; abstract has no numbers.

sources.title: Phantom-Data: Towards a General Subject-Consistent Video Generation Dataset
claims: About one million identity-consistent cross-pair examples, mined from 53 million videos and 3 billion images in three stages.
Cross-pair data (reference taken from a different scene than the target) reduces copy-paste of the reference.
Training on it improves prompt alignment and quality while keeping identity consistency on par with in-pair training.

sources.title: BindWeave: Subject-Consistent Video Generation via Cross-Modal Integration
claims: A multimodal LLM paired with a diffusion transformer grounds each entity role, attributes and interactions before generating.
Handles one or several subjects; reported better than open and commercial models on the OpenS2V benchmark.

sources.title: MV-S2V: Multi-View Subject-Consistent Video Generation
claims: Takes several reference views of one subject to reach 3D-level consistency instead of a single view.
Temporally Shifted RoPE separates different subjects and views within the context.
Uses a synthetic data pipeline plus a small real-world dataset.

sources.title: VACE: All-in-One Video Creation and Editing
claims: One model for reference-to-video, video-to-video editing and masked editing, with inputs packed as a Video Condition Unit.
A Context Adapter injects the task concept; performance is on par with task-specific models.

sources.title: Adapting VACE for Real-Time Autoregressive Video Diffusion
claims: Moves reference frames to a parallel conditioning path so chunk size and KV cache stay fixed; reuses VACE weights without training.
VACE adds 20-30% latency at 1.3B and 14B scales for structural control and inpainting, with negligible VRAM cost.
Reference-to-video fidelity is severely degraded compared with batch VACE because of causal attention limits.

sources.title: VBench: Comprehensive Benchmark Suite for Video Generative Models
claims: 16 hierarchical dimensions, including subject identity consistency, motion smoothness and temporal flickering.
Includes human preference annotations used to check that each metric agrees with human perception.

sources.title: VBench++: Comprehensive and Versatile Benchmark Suite for Video Generative Models
claims: Keeps the 16 dimensions and adds an image-to-video suite with adaptive aspect ratios.
Also scores trustworthiness of video models; open leaderboard.

sources.title: VBench-2.0: Advancing Video Generation Benchmark Suite for Intrinsic Faithfulness
claims: Argues earlier metrics measure only surface plausibility, not adherence to real-world principles.
Five dimensions: human fidelity, controllability, creativity, physics, commonsense, with finer sub-capabilities.
Combines VLM/LLM judges with specialist anomaly detectors, validated against human annotation.

sources.title: T2V-CompBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Compositional Text-to-Video Generation
claims: Seven compositional categories including attribute binding, spatial relations, motion, interaction and numeracy; 1400 prompts.
Three evaluators: MLLM-based, detection-based and tracking-based, checked against human judgments.
Concludes current models find compositional generation very difficult.

sources.title: EvalCrafter: Benchmarking and Evaluating Large Video Generation Models
claims: 700 prompts from real user data; 17 objective metrics over visual quality, content, motion and text alignment.
Metrics are re-weighted to match user opinion and the combined score tracks human preference better than a plain average.

sources.title: VideoScore: Building Automatic Metrics to Simulate Fine-grained Human Feedback for Video Generation
claims: VideoFeedback: human multi-aspect scores for 37.6K videos from 11 generators.
VideoScore reaches 77.1 Spearman correlation with humans on the test set, about 50 points above earlier metrics.
Also correlates better on held-out EvalCrafter, GenAI-Bench and VBench; proposed as a proxy rater and feedback signal.

sources.title: Movie Gen: A Cast of Media Foundation Models
claims: Largest video model has 30B parameters and a 73K-token context, making 16-second clips at 16 fps in 1080p with synchronized audio.
Includes personalized video from a user image and instruction-based editing.
sources.notes: Benchmark prompt set (Movie Gen Bench) not read.

sources.title: VideoPhy: Evaluating Physical Commonsense for Video Generation
claims: Tests physics in solid-solid, solid-fluid and fluid-fluid interactions with human evaluation.
The best model, CogVideoX-5B, satisfies both caption and physics in only 39.6% of videos.
Proposes the automatic evaluator VideoCon-Physics.

sources.title: VideoPhy-2: A Challenging Action-Centric Physical Commonsense Evaluation in Video Generation
claims: 200 real-world actions; humans score semantic adherence and physical plausibility.
Best model reaches only 22% joint performance on the hard subset.
Models fail most on conservation laws (mass, momentum); releases VideoPhy-AutoEval.

sources.title: Physics-IQ Verified
claims: Audit of the Physics-IQ benchmark: prompts and ground truth refined, 57.6% of samples refined, 34.8% of prompts improved.
Re-scoring six image-to-video models changes the ranking moderately (Kendall tau 0.46), so published rankings are fragile.

sources.title: Sci-VBench: Evaluating Knowledge- and Reasoning-Intensive Video Generation in Science Domains
claims: 1,253 expert-annotated examples over 60 subjects and four disciplines, 16 models tested.
Perceptual-quality scores are tightly clustered across models, while prompt grounding and causal correctness vary widely.

sources.title: KeyVID: Keyframe-Aware Video Diffusion for Audio-Synchronized Visual Animation
claims: Generates keyframes first, then a motion interpolator fills frames between them using masked frame conditioning.
Conditioning on several keyframes, not only the first frame, is the design that improves sync.
sources.notes: Seen only in a search result summary.

sources.title: ViBiDSampler: Enhancing Video Interpolation Using Bidirectional Diffusion Sampler
claims: Image-to-video models are built for a start frame only, so end-frame conditioning needs an adapted sampler.
Bidirectional sampling from both ends gives keyframe interpolation without fine-tuning.
sources.notes: Seen only in a search result summary.

sources.title: Generative Inbetweening: Adapting Image-to-Video Models for Keyframe Interpolation
claims: Adapts a pretrained image-to-video model to fill motion between two input keyframes.
sources.notes: Seen only in a search result summary.

sources.title: DiffuseSlide: Training-Free High Frame Rate Video Generation Diffusion
claims: Generates low frame rate latents, interpolates linearly, then denoises with a sliding window.
Conditioning only on the first keyframe is too weak for later frames, which the sliding window compensates for.
sources.notes: Seen only in a search result summary.

sources.title: Adapting Image-to-Video Diffusion Models for Large-Motion Frame Interpolation
claims: A conditional encoder takes features of the first and last frame to steer an image-to-video model when motion between them is large.
sources.notes: Seen only in a search result summary.

sources.title: A Survey on Long Video Generation: Challenges, Methods, and Prospects
claims: Groups methods into divide-and-conquer and temporal-autoregressive paradigms.
Covers temporal-spatial consistency, content continuity and diversity; frame skipping and motion inconsistency remain open.
sources.notes: Seen only in a search result summary.

sources.title: A Survey on Long-Video Storytelling Generation: Architectures, Consistency, and Cinematic Quality
claims: Reviews 32 papers and proposes a taxonomy of six architectural styles.
Multi-subject videos still struggle with character consistency and motion coherence; some methods reach about 150 s but with frame redundancy.
sources.notes: Seen only in a search result summary.

sources.title: GenScale: A Benchmark for Relative Object Scale in Image Generation and Editing
claims: Benchmark of 900 images and 1,643 anchor-target size relations; no current generator or editor reliably draws plausible relative scale.
Plausible = within about 20% error on a five-point ordinal scale; judge agrees with human raters (kappa 0.82).
Common-object generation: best model 56.5% plausible, SD3.5-Large 31.0%; FLUX.1 Kontext-dev 63.2% on human-product scale.
Of failed images, only 20.4% start plausible; best editor lifts them to 53.3%, others to 26-33%; editors follow explicit resize orders better than they find errors alone.
Rescale agent: box the target, estimate a resize factor, SAM 2 cut-out, Depth Anything V2, re-insert (Insert Anything); human-judged plausible pairs rose 11.7% to 88.3% on representative cases.
sources.notes: Read the abstract page and the HTML up to about 100k characters; the last 130k characters (appendix) were not read. Numbers are the paper's own.

sources.title: DLEBench: Evaluating Small-scale Object Editing Ability for Instruction-based Image Editing Model
claims: 1,889 samples, seven instruction types, target objects covering only 1% to 10% of the image area; ten editing models tested.
Reports significant gaps in editing small objects, so a small character in a wide picture is a weak spot for instruction-based editors.

sources.title: MoFu: Scale-Aware Modulation and Fourier Fusion for Multi-Subject Video Generation
claims: Names scale inconsistency as a main failure of multi-subject reference-to-video: reference images come at different zoom levels, so subjects turn out unnaturally large or small.
Fix: an LLM reads scale cues from the prompt and modulates features; a loss on area ratios keeps scale stable regardless of reference order.
MoFu-Bench has 1,000 subject-text pairs (up to 3 references). ScaleScore is a GPT-4o rating from 10 sampled frames: Phantom 0.536, VACE 0.547, MAGREF 0.511, MoFu 0.585.
sources.notes: Table numbers read from the arXiv HTML. ScaleScore is an LLM judge, not a measured box ratio.

sources.title: EntityBench: Towards Entity-Consistent Long-Range Multi-Shot Video Generation
claims: 140 episodes, 2,491 shots, up to 50 shots per episode; cross-shot entity consistency degrades sharply as the gap between an entity's appearances grows.

Measures with GroundingDINO presence, DINOv2 cosine to a per-entity centroid and a multimodal LLM judged against a registry description; only accurate appearances enter cross-shot scoring (a fidelity gate).
A memory bank of verified references per entity gave the best character fidelity of the four systems compared.
sources.notes: Thresholds of the gate and the presence test were not visible in the part read. Only the first 100k characters of the HTML were read.

sources.title: Ctrl-V: Higher Fidelity Video Generation with Bounding-Box Controlled Object Motion
claims: Video diffusion (fine-tuned Stable Video Diffusion) conditioned on 2D or 3D boxes rendered in pixel space; a second model predicts the box trajectories.
Validated on driving datasets (KITTI, Virtual-KITTI 2, BDD100k, nuScenes), not on story scenes.

sources.title: TrailBlazer: Trajectory Control for Diffusion-Based Video Generation
claims: Steers a subject with simple boxes by editing attention maps of a pretrained text-to-video model, no training.
A growing box makes the subject appear to move toward the camera, so box size is the scale control and a moving box changes apparent size on purpose.

sources.title: Boximator: Generating Rich and Controllable Motions for Video Synthesis
claims: Plug-in module for existing video diffusion models; hard boxes select objects in the first frame, hard or soft boxes then fix position, shape or path in later frames.
Reports better FVD, higher box-alignment scores and human preference over the base models; no numbers in the abstract.

sources.title: Direct-a-Video: Customized Video Generation with User-Directed Camera Movement and Object Motion
claims: Controls object motion (attention modulation) and camera pan and zoom (separate temporal layers with numeric parameters) independently, so a camera move is not left to the prompt.

sources.title: GLIGEN: Open-Set Grounded Text-to-Image Generation
claims: Adds grounding boxes tied to concepts to a frozen text-to-image model through gated trainable layers, so a named object is placed in a chosen region at a chosen size.
Zero-shot layout-to-image on COCO and LVIS beats supervised layout baselines by a large margin.

sources.title: Be Yourself: Bounded Attention for Multi-Subject Text-to-Image Generation
claims: Layout-to-image methods leak features between similar-looking subjects in the denoising attention; a training-free bound on information flow keeps each subject its own and matches the layout better.

sources.title: Training-Free Layout Control with Cross-Attention Guidance
claims: Steers where objects appear by guiding cross-attention at sampling time, no fine-tuning; backward guidance (gradient on the latent) beat forward guidance and earlier layout methods on three benchmarks.

sources.title: Adding Conditional Control to Text-to-Image Diffusion Models (ControlNet)
claims: Locks a pretrained image model and adds a trainable copy with zero-initialised convolutions; conditions include edges, depth, segmentation and pose, alone or combined.

sources.title: Rebalancing Reference Frame Dominance to Improve Motion in Image-to-Video Models (DyMoS)
claims: Image-to-video clips are more static than text-to-video because later frames over-attend to the reference frame; DyMoS rebalances this in the first 20-25% of denoising with one scalar.
VBench-I2V dynamic degree: Wan 2.2-14B 51.7 to 64.8, Wan 2.1 48.7 to 54.5, HunyuanVideo-1.5 48.0 to 55.3, CogVideoX-5B 30.9 to 52.9; flow magnitude up 28-32%.
Too large a scalar costs appearance consistency; the paper does not discuss camera drift.
sources.notes: Last 32k characters of the HTML were not read.

sources.title: Follow-Your-Click: Open-domain Regional Image Animation via Short Prompts
claims: Animates only the region a click selects, with a first-frame masking strategy and flow-based motion magnitude control for the speed of the target movement.
Reported on 7 baselines and 8 metrics; the abstract gives no numbers for the speed control.

sources.title: MotionStone: Decoupled Motion Intensity Modulation with Diffusion Transformer for Image-to-Video Generation
claims: A learned estimator scores object motion and camera motion intensity separately (pairwise contrastive training), and the score becomes a control input for image-to-video.
Camera and object motion strength can be set independently, which a text prompt cannot do.

sources.title: CamI2V: Camera-Controlled Image-to-Video Diffusion Model
claims: Temporal attention only links features at the same pixel position, so large camera shifts break cross-frame consistency; epipolar attention along matching lines improves camera controllability by 25.64% on RealEstate10K.

sources.title: RealCam-I2V: Real-World Image-to-Video Generation with Interactive Complex Camera Control
claims: Camera parameters are ambiguous in scale for an arbitrary photo; a monocular metric depth estimate turns relative camera motion into absolute scale so the same move means the same on every image.

sources.title: CameraCtrl: Enabling Camera Control for Text-to-Video Generation
claims: Plug-in camera pose control for a video diffusion model; training on clips with diverse camera motion and an appearance close to the base model improved control and generalisation.

sources.title: MotionMaster: Training-free Camera Motion Transfer For Video Generation
claims: Separates camera motion from object motion in temporal attention (background motion, Poisson equation in the moving-object region); shows camera and object movement can be pulled apart in generated video.

sources.title: MotionPro: A Precise Motion Controller for Image-to-Video Generation
claims: Region-wise trajectories plus a motion mask (object or camera motion) modulate denoising; MC-Bench has 1.1K user-annotated image-trajectory pairs.

sources.title: KeyFrame-Compass: Towards Comprehensive Evaluation of Keyframe-Conditioned Video Generation
claims: 386 samples; scores keyframe presence, fidelity, temporal order, localization, persistence and uniqueness across nine systems.
Finds a trade-off between hitting the keyframes and natural video, and worse results as keyframes get denser.

sources.title: Anchoring and Rescaling Attention for Semantically Coherent Inbetweening
claims: Earlier first-last-frame models struggle as keyframes get sparser or motion larger; a keyframe-anchored attention bias and rescaled temporal RoPE improve frame consistency and pace stability without training (TGI-Bench).

sources.title: Gemini Omni Flash guide
claims: Extension appends to the end only and uses the last 10 seconds of the input as context; each turn adds 3 to 10 seconds, up to 30 seconds total.
If a character appeared only before the last 10 seconds, name it again or pass it as a reference image.
First and last frame interpolation takes two images and 3 to 10 seconds; image-to-video uses one image.
Multi-turn edits build on the previous result; adding 'keep everything else the same' preserves the rest of the scene.
Up to 3 reference images per character for up to 2 characters, 6 images in total.
Say 'single continuous shot' or 'no scene cuts' to avoid unwanted cuts.
sources.notes: Last 2260 characters of the page were not read.

sources.title: Edit videos & build scenes in Flow
claims: Extending a clip: choose a duration, describe how the action continues, add up to 3 image references for consistency.
A paused frame can be saved as an image and reused as an ingredient, start frame or end frame.
Scenebuilder arranges, reorders and trims whole clips with handles; it does not edit inside a clip.
Edits keep earlier versions in a History panel, and the original is not overwritten.

sources.title: A Guide to Kling Turbo Start End Frame
claims: Keep lighting consistent across the start and end frames; a sharp lighting jump can cause flicker.
Avoid large perspective changes between the two frames, e.g. wide-angle start with telephoto end.
The end frame should show a related but different state with the same subject identity.
Five second clips transition more cleanly; ten seconds suits dramatic changes.
The start frame also sets the aspect ratio of the whole video.
sources.notes: Reseller blog; the page does not cover chaining.

sources.title: Google Flow SceneBuilder vs Luma Scenes
claims: Luma Scenes generates all keyframes together in one context and shows a storyboard for review before rendering video.
One keyframe can be regenerated without touching approved ones.
Flow SceneBuilder assembles separately generated clips and relies on character ingredients and extension for continuity.
sources.notes: Written by a competitor; treat the comparison as marketing.

sources.title: Veo 3 Video verlaengern (long video guide)
claims: Via the Gemini API each extension adds 7 seconds, up to 20 extensions, about 148 seconds in all (as the article states).
Drift is clothing colour, background and lighting shifting slightly between segments and adding up; check after every extension.
Repeat the full character description in every prompt; shortened descriptions let long hair become short.
Trim one or two overlapping frames at each join.
Starting each extension from a clean reference still reduces drift.
sources.notes: Numbers are for the older Veo 3 API; the article does not measure degradation.

sources.title: Kling V3: The Essentials
claims: End image works only in the single-scene Standard Prompt workflow, not with Multi-Prompting.
Multi-Prompt builds up to five shots in one generation, each with its own prompt and duration; the main prompt box must stay empty.
An Element needs an extra reference image besides the start image or it errors.
sources.notes: Platform help page, not Kling itself.

sources.title: Wan2.1-FLF2V-14B-720P model card
claims: The first-last-frame model outputs 720P only; the aspect ratio follows the input images.
It takes a first and a last image plus a prompt describing style, motion, background and camera.
Chinese prompts work better because training captions were mainly Chinese.

sources.title: AniDoc: Animation Creation Made Easier
claims: Given a character image plus start and end sketches, it generates a temporally consistent in-between animation.
Correspondence matching keeps it robust when the pose differs between the reference and a frame.
sources.notes: Abstract only; line-art workflow, only loosely related.

sources.title: My Sora2 Workflow for Continuous Video Generation
claims: Loop: extract the last frame, write the next scene prompt from that frame plus the earlier context, generate, stitch.
The author calls the last-frame handoff what keeps continuity 'surprisingly stable'.
An optional reference image anchors the look from the start; deciding when to hold a shot versus add a beat is left open.
sources.notes: Short post; no failure analysis.

sources.title: LTX 2.3 first, middle and last frame in ComfyUI
claims: Keyframes can sit at first, middle (frame 24 of 49) and last (frame 48) positions.
Frame count must be 8n+1 and reference images must match the target size, divisible by 32.
Add Guide is soft and lets motion flow; Inplace locks the frame nearly exactly but frees less motion.
Put a middle keyframe at the point where a transition happens.

sources.title: How to Use LTX-2 for Keyframe Interpolation
claims: LTX-2 KeyframeInterpolationPipeline renders at half resolution then upsamples 2x with a distilled LoRA.
Keyframe images are given with a weight each; the article does not state a keyframe limit.
sources.notes: Auto-generated code walkthrough; paths unverified.

sources.title: How to use Keyframes
claims: A keyframe sets the start or end frame; a prompt can guide the transition between them.
Extend can take an image keyframe as the destination; extended videos run up to 9 seconds from a default 4 second clip.

sources.title: LTXVAddGuide node
claims: Guide frame index must be a multiple of 8 for inputs of 9 or more frames; negative values count from the end.
Guide strength runs 0 to 10, default 1.0 (full conditioning).

sources.title: ConsistI2V: Enhancing Visual Consistency for Image-to-Video Generation
claims: Attention spanning the first frame preserves subject, background and style; noise initialised from the first frame's low frequencies preserves layout.
The same ideas are applied to long auto-regressive generation; evaluation uses a new I2V-Bench.
sources.notes: Abstract only.

sources.title: Captain Cinema: Towards Short Movie Generation
claims: Stage one plans keyframes for the whole story to hold scenes and characters consistent; stage two generates motion between them.
Authors claim narrative-consistent short movies; no numbers in the abstract.
sources.notes: Abstract only.

sources.title: Runway Gen-4 References: a creator workflow
claims: Use a simple scene reference with clean walls and low clutter; busy scenes can melt or warp.
Change only one variable per shot (location, camera or time of day) so drift can be traced.
Change location by swapping the Scene reference while keeping the character reference.
sources.notes: Third-party blog.

sources.title: How to Use Kling 3.0 Pro
claims: Multi-shot: each shot 1 to 15 seconds in one multi_prompt call; total is the sum of the shots.
end_image_url sets a target final frame; suggested uses are morphs, camera moves to a fixed frame, loops and connecting two scenes.
Elements (tagged @Element1...) hold characters or objects across multi-shot sequences.
The author's testing: clips of 3 to 6 seconds keep motion tighter; longer clips drift more.
sources.notes: API reseller guide.

sources.title: Kling 3.0 Turbo guide
claims: Multi-shot syntax is a shot number, seconds and a prompt per shot; one to six shots, each at least 1 second.
Keep each shot prompt under about 500 characters and to a single beat.
Starting from a still fixes the look before motion begins.

sources.title: LTX 2.5 First & Last Frame to Video
claims: Match aspect ratio, horizon and subject scale in both frames or the model warps geometry.
Describe both the opening beat and the end state in the prompt.
Very high guidance can overconstrain motion; lower it if motion looks stiff.

sources.title: How to chain AI video clips into one shot without the hidden stutter
claims: Matched frames do not match velocity: clips ease to a stop, so chaining from the last frame restarts from rest and hitches.
Generate longer than needed (e.g. 5 to 6 s for 4 s) and take the chaining frame before the deceleration zone, often the last 10 to 15 percent.
Decide the seed frame for the next clip at planning time; the author says this cut re-chaining from four tries to one.

sources.title: Why do the first frames of an AI-extended clip look wrong
claims: Extension regenerates frames around the join; the first two frames are often duplicated, smeared or off-model.
Start the new clip at frame three; a frame-only extension also loses character, location and camera context.
For long chains use reference-to-video with locked character and location references.
sources.notes: Vendor FAQ.

sources.title: Stable Video Infinity: Infinite-Length Video Generation with Error Recycling
claims: Authors name the cause of drift as a train/test mismatch: clean training inputs but imperfect self-generated conditioning at test time.
Error-recycling fine-tuning feeds the model its own past errors; authors report state of the art on three benchmarks.
sources.notes: Abstract only.

sources.title: Error Analyses of Auto-Regressive Video Diffusion Models
claims: Two failure modes: history forgetting and temporal degradation.
More past frames in the context reduce forgetting (proved), and the two failures are strongly correlated in experiments.
sources.notes: Abstract only.

sources.title: TokenTrim: Inference-Time Token Pruning for Autoregressive Long Video Generation
claims: Authors argue drift comes from corrupted tokens reused as conditioning, not from low model capacity.
Removing unstable tokens from the context at inference improves long-horizon consistency (authors' claim).
sources.notes: Abstract only; author names not read.

sources.title: How to colour-match AI video clips
claims: Each generation is graded on its own, so five shots of one scene can come back with five palettes.
State colour temperature as a number (3200K, 6500K) and repeat one palette line in every prompt.
Generate the establishing wide first and use it as the reference for closer shots; grade in a dedicated pass before editing.

sources.title: Pack and Force Your Memory: Long-form and Consistent Video Generation
claims: MemoryPack retrieves short and long term context using text and image as global guidance, aiming at minute-level consistency at linear cost.
Direct Forcing aligns training with inference to cut error propagation (authors' claim).
sources.notes: Abstract only.

sources.title: HiAR: hierarchical denoising for long autoregressive video
claims: Conditioning each block on context at the same noise level, not a fully clean one, is said to reduce error build-up.
On VBench with 20 second videos the authors report the lowest temporal drift among compared methods.
sources.notes: Abstract only; title wording is a paraphrase.

sources.title: Flowception
claims: Inserting and denoising frames in any order is said to reduce error build-up versus strictly autoregressive models.
The same process covers image-to-video and frame interpolation.
sources.notes: Abstract only.

sources.title: Test-Time Correction for distilled autoregressive video diffusion
claims: Test-Time Correction uses the first frame as a stable anchor to keep long generation consistent, with no training.
Authors report it matches training-based methods on 30 second benchmarks.
sources.notes: Abstract only; title is a paraphrase.

sources.title: Multi-shot video stitching API
claims: Scale all clips to one resolution, frame rate and aspect ratio before joining; mismatches show as stutter or letterboxing.
Concatenation does not fix continuity, it only places the mismatch back to back.
Use crossfades or wipes when shots clash; add captions after stitching.

sources.title: The Transition Troubleshooter: Fixing Video Clip Gaps
claims: Extend clips slightly past the cut and use a short crossfade to mask small differences.
Reuse the same wording for fixed character details and make short clips, reviewing each before the next.
sources.notes: Vendor blog.

sources.title: How to Fix Background Artifacts in AI Video
claims: Check a clip at normal speed and frame by frame; a repair can look clean when paused and jitter in playback.
Log the first and last frames where a defect appears and lock the approved parts before regenerating.
sources.notes: Vendor tutorial.

sources.title: Kling AI video post-processing with FFmpeg
claims: The author says Kling colour balance can drift within a 5 to 10 second clip, about 5600K toward 5100K.
A deflicker filter normalises luminance across a window of frames.
sources.notes: Colour numbers are one author's observation.

sources.title: MAViS: A Multi-Agent Framework for Long-Sequence Video Storytelling
claims: Agents cover script writing, shot design, character modeling, keyframes, animation and audio.
Each stage runs an Explore, Examine, Enhance loop (the 3E principle).
The authors propose script-writing guidelines so scripts suit generative tools.
sources.notes: Abstract page only; no numbers or shot format were visible.

sources.title: Hollywood Town: Long-Video Generation via Cross-Modal Multi-Agent Orchestration
claims: Graph-based hierarchical agents modeled on film production (OmniAgent).
Cyclic graphs with limited retries let later stages send feedback to earlier ones.
Agents with too little context can hold a temporary group discussion (hypergraph nodes).
sources.notes: Abstract only; no results visible.

sources.title: STORYANCHORS: Generating Consistent Multi-Scene Story Frames for Long-Form Narratives
claims: A bidirectional story generator uses both past and future frames so scenes stay consistent.
Story frames are generated separately from video synthesis and can be edited and extended.
Claims narrative consistency on par with GPT-4o, stated without numbers.
sources.notes: Abstract only.

sources.title: AI micro-drama hooks and cliffhangers
claims: Open on a face mid-reaction, a shock line or a reveal already moving; not on an establishing shot, title card or walk-in.
A 60 s episode has a cold open (0-3 s), one reversal near 30 s and a cliffhanger as the final shot.
One reversal per 60 s is a ceiling: two flips and neither lands.
End one beat before resolution; write reversals as visual beats (an expression changing) not dialogue.
sources.notes: Vendor blog about vertical micro-dramas; the cost example is one reported case, not a rule.

sources.title: Crafting short films that hook in under 60 seconds
claims: Build a sub-60 s film on one idea: a choice, a moment of truth, a twist or a visual metaphor.
Hook in the first 3-5 s; use actions, reactions and details instead of dialogue.
Pick the target emotion first and write backward from it; one turn of expectation is enough.
sources.notes: Informal blog; gives no shot counts.

sources.title: The ideal YouTube Shorts length and format for retention
claims: Claims 15-30 s Shorts retain best; storytelling pieces run 30-45 s with a new visual or story beat every 5-7 s.
Claims 50-60% of drop-off happens in the first 3 s; start with the most compelling moment, not context.
Advises drafting then cutting the script by about 30%; write the 3 s hook and 3 s payoff first.
sources.notes: Vendor; figures are unsourced author estimates, treat as directional.

sources.title: Runway's film festival marked an inflection point for AI movies
claims: The 2024 Grand Prix 'Get Me Out' paired live-action emotion with AI visual effects.
A producer said AI should stay in the background and not pull focus from character or story.
Best entries had narrative foundations, with AI assets integrated into the story.
sources.notes: Winner running times were not given.

sources.title: How to win the Runway AI Film Festival
claims: Judges score 1-10 on composition, narrative and artistic cohesion, originality and AI technique (per this page's account of the rules).
The page argues story beats spectacle and suggests a test: can the film be compelling in one sentence.
Advises locking the script before generating.
sources.notes: Third-party site; rules unverified against Runway.

sources.title: AI video storyboarding: plan shot sequences before generation
claims: If a shot card holds several movements, split it into shots with one primary action each.
Estimate clip count by dividing runtime into beat durations; quick reactions get less time, reveals more.
Build a continuity bible (character, location, lighting, style, motion); review each clip against its card and change one element.
sources.notes: Vendor tutorial; no numeric rules.

sources.title: Storyboarding AI video: a repeatable workflow for consistent multi-shot sequences
claims: State the story in one sentence; if you cannot, it is too big for a first project.
Each clip is one shot with one action; limit recurring characters to one or two.
Generate the hardest or most important shot first; if it fails, revise the story before paying for easy shots.
Cut on motion (end one clip mid-movement, start the next moving) to hide small mismatches.

sources.title: Co-Writing Screenplays and Theatre Scripts with Language Models (Dramatron)
claims: Hierarchical prompt chaining generates title, characters, story beats, locations and dialogue so output stays coherent over a long form.
15 theatre and film professionals co-wrote with it; findings are qualitative interviews, no scores.

sources.title: Re3: Generating Longer Stories With Recursive Reprompting and Revision
claims: Plan first, then write passages with the plan and story state re-inserted, rerank continuations, then edit.
Human judges found a coherent overall plot 14 points more often and premise relevance 20 points more often than direct generation.
sources.notes: Stories over 2,000 words; text only.

sources.title: Kishotenketsu
claims: Four parts: introduction, development, twist, conclusion; the twist comes at the third part and can change the genre.
The structure does not centre on conflict, though stories using it can contain conflict.
If a story turns several times, the largest turn is the twist.

sources.title: The 22 rules of storytelling, according to Pixar
claims: Story spine: a routine, then a disruption, then consequences that each cause the next, until the outcome.
Decide the ending before the middle; find the most economical telling of the essence and build out.
Cut side paths and merge characters; accidents that solve the problem for the hero feel like cheating.
sources.notes: Rules came from Pixar storyboard artist Emma Coats' 2011 tweets.

sources.title: Ultimate prompting guide for Veo 3.1
claims: Veo 3.1 makes 4, 6 or 8 s clips.
Spoken lines go in quotation marks; sound effects and ambience are described separately.
Its dialogue example uses one line per generation, the reply in a separate prompt.
Timestamp prompting directs several shots inside one 8 s generation.
sources.notes: Page gives no explicit one-action rule.

sources.title: Kishotenketsu: the structure that grabs attention without conflict
claims: The twist must genuinely surprise and recontextualise the earlier parts.
Do not rush the development part; the conclusion should feel surprising and inevitable.
Does not address short-form length.

sources.title: AI video storyboard workflow
claims: Plan 3-7 shots, each with one role (hook, context, detail, proof, transition, final frame).
Generate 2-4 variations per shot before moving on; judge each clip against its storyboard role.
Use image-to-video when a character must stay accurate; change one variable at a time when a clip fails.
sources.notes: Marketing-ad oriented; no regeneration rates.

sources.title: How to make a one-minute AI video shot by shot
claims: Six 10 s clips is a ceiling for one minute, not a target; use more, shorter shots so the edit sets pace.
Clips run 2-10 s; pick the shortest that holds the action and leave trim handles.
Avoid asking a 5 s clip for a journey, a transformation and a final pose; shots that do not advance the one-sentence change feel like unrelated demos.

sources.title: Generating extended AI clips
claims: For continuous action the page prefers one extended take (follow a character through a door) over cutting to a reaction.
Longer clips risk morphing and cost more; test cheaply at low resolution first.
sources.notes: Page has no explicit chaining rules.

sources.title: DirectorBench: Diagnosing Long-Form Video Generation with Personalized Multi-Agent Evaluation
claims: Tested four long-form workflows and six LLMs: transition quality averaged 0.256, best workflow 0.356 (the between-unit bottleneck).
Prompt-level demand fulfilment averaged 0.71.
Scores five dimensions: script, visual, audio, cross-modal, stability.

sources.title: MSVBench: Towards Human-Level Evaluation of Multi-Shot Video Generation
claims: Across 20 methods, current models act as visual interpolators rather than true world models despite strong fidelity.
The hybrid benchmark reaches 94.4% Spearman correlation with human judgments.

sources.title: ViMax: Agentic Video Generation
claims: Uses a hierarchical narrative engine with retrieval for global story coherence.
Tracks character and environment state across scene boundaries.
VLM agents check narrative coherence and visual fidelity.
sources.notes: Abstract only; no results.

sources.title: What works and what goes wrong in an AI film
claims: AI does short single-location scenes and moody light well.
Common failures: faces, clothes or places change between shots; odd hands; strange crowd faces; garbled sign text; lip sync; cut-off sentences.
sources.notes: The clip-length and story rules the page promises are in other lessons.

sources.title: The biggest mistake beginners make with AI filmmaking
claims: Biggest mistake is generating before the story is written shot by shot; clips look good alone and do not fit.
Write one sentence per shot saying what it must accomplish, and note what carries over (light, position, time, props).
Author reports planned shots took 1-2 attempts and improvised ones 4-7.
sources.notes: Single author's experience.

sources.title: Exploring the rule of three
claims: Children enjoy predictable patterns; a phrase repeated three times aids rhythm and memory.
By the third repetition children know what is coming and feel satisfaction in leading it.

sources.title: What is show, don't tell in writing and film
claims: Show emotion through the body (a furrowed brow, a hesitant step) not stated feelings.
A small object can carry fear or tension in place of dialogue; framing (close-up vs wide) shows inner state.

sources.title: From script to screen: story videos with AI tools
claims: A 30 s emotional story can be six to eight clips of about 5 s; default to 5 s per clip.
List beats as setup, rising tension, reversal, payoff, each as a scene card; give each clip one primary verb plus one camera move.
If a sound or event drives a later beat, mention it again in the next scene so the motion makes sense.
Generate scene 1 alone and lock its look before writing later scenes.
sources.notes: Vendor tutorial.

sources.title: AI storyboard to video
claims: Each shot card needs number, description, visual reference, motion direction and estimated duration.
Says to expect to regenerate 30-40% of shots for consistency; generate one shot at a time with the same model and references.
sources.notes: Its own motion example packs several actions, so it does not follow a one-verb rule.

sources.title: YouTube Shorts with AI: the 3-second hook system
claims: The hook must resolve by the 3 s mark; keep logos and intros out of the first second; avoid slow fades and beautiful-landscape AI establishing shots as openers.
Do not rely on audio for the hook, since many viewers watch muted; use readable captions.
Create speed in the edit with shorter cuts toward the payoff, not the word 'fast' in the prompt (author's experience).
sources.notes: Affiliate link disclosed; benchmarks unsourced.

sources.title: Hook engineering: the first 3 seconds in short-form video
claims: Suggests hooks land in 1.5-2 s on TikTok, 1-2 s on Reels, 2-3 s on Shorts; the first frame must work on mute.
Reports average scroll-decision windows of 1.4-2.3 s, from unnamed platform data.
Most figures are the author's own unpublished datasets.
sources.notes: Promotes the author's tool; treat numbers as unverified.

sources.title: Looping logic: how Oswald uses story structure to comfort young viewers
claims: A critic argues a structure that returns to a familiar safe space lowers anxiety for young viewers.
sources.notes: Search summary only; critic's view, not a study.

sources.title: How to script a 2-minute kids story that holds toddler attention
