claims: Vendor advice: let a narrator carry the story with only short character lines, and read the script aloud to test it.
sources.notes: Search summary only; vendor marketing.

sources.title: 5 tips for getting started with Flow
claims: Flow clips are 8 seconds; Ingredients to Video takes up to three reusable elements (characters, objects, style) per prompt.
Frames to Video starts from an uploaded image or a frame reused from an earlier generation, for smoother transitions.
Scenebuilder is a storyboard for clips; Jump To moves a subject to a new setting, Extend continues the action from the final frames.
For multi-clip consistency, tell Gemini to repeat the essential details from earlier prompts.
At the time, Ingredients, Jump To and Extend worked only with Veo 2, not Veo 3.
sources.notes: Vendor post; model support has since changed.

sources.title: AI filmmaking pipeline: script to screen
claims: Seven stages in order: script, storyboard/pre-viz, character design, video generation, voice and audio, edit/post, distribution.
Suggests a cheap image model for daily storyboard frames and a stronger one only for hero shots.
Nano Banana Pro Edit is quoted at $0.15 per edit and up to 14 reference images; Kling 3.0 at up to 6 cuts per generation.
Gives no take counts per shot.
sources.notes: Vendor blog; prices may have moved.

sources.title: How to make AI films: short film guide 2026
claims: Plan 8-15 scenes of 10-30 seconds, each with 2-5 shots of 3-5 second clips.
Generate 3-5 variations per shot, then trim each clip to its strongest 2-3 seconds.
A 2-3 minute short typically needs 50-150 video generations.
Edit mostly with straight cuts and apply one unified colour grade before sound.
sources.notes: Vendor blog promoting its own tools.

sources.title: AI filmmaking tools 2026
claims: Use a 3-4 tool stack, each tool matched to the stage it does best.
Build 4-6 character reference images (poses, lighting) before video and reuse them in every prompt; improves but does not guarantee consistency.
Veo 3.1 fast mode from $0.15 per second; author says Kling costs about 40 percent of Runway Gen-4 per second.
Estimates $40-120 of generation for a 3-5 minute short, depending on discarded takes.
Multi-speaker dialogue still needs manual sync in post.
sources.notes: Author reports three weeks of testing; figures unverified.

sources.title: Veo 3 Flow full tutorial
claims: Flow organises a project as generations you can browse; frames-to-video takes first and last frames from uploads or the Ingredients drawer.
Scene Builder arranges clips into longer sequences; Jump To generates the next clip from the previous one.
Editing tools include trimming with handles, Extend, saving frames, reordering clips and downloading the scene.
Camera paths can be previewed before generating.
sources.notes: Read from the chapter list and summary, not the video.

sources.title: How three filmmakers created Sora's latest videos
claims: Shy Kids generated many separate clips for Air Head, edited them together and post-processed them, including fixing the balloon face.
The director calls Sora a slot machine: keeping the character consistent was only mostly successful.
Music and voice-over were made by the team itself.
Another filmmaker warns that details you liked in a low-resolution preview can change when re-run at high resolution.

sources.title: Wan2.2 workflows in ComfyUI
claims: The 5B hybrid model with native offloading is said to run on about 8 GB of VRAM; 14B models use separate high-noise and low-noise files.
First/last frame uses WanFirstLastFrameToVideo with two Load Image nodes and the same model files as image-to-video.
Resolution and length are set on the latent/first-last-frame node; about 720p is suggested if VRAM allows.
A 4-step Lightx2v speed LoRA exists but its instructions were still marked as in preparation.
sources.notes: Date approximate to the Wan 2.2 release month.

sources.title: OpenAI backs Critterz
claims: Critterz is an animated feature with about 30 people, a budget under $30 million and a planned nine-month schedule.
Human artists draw the initial designs which feed the AI tools; human voice actors perform the characters.
Humans stay deeply involved partly because purely AI-generated work generally cannot be copyrighted.

sources.title: Introducing Runway Gen-4
claims: One reference image is enough to keep a character consistent across scenes, without fine-tuning.
Coverage workflow: supply references and describe composition to get multiple angles of one scene.
Runway published short films and music videos made with Gen-4 to show narrative use.
sources.notes: Promotional; claims not independently verified.

sources.title: Sora's Air Head: plenty of human post-processing
claims: Hundreds of 10-20 second clips were generated; the post lead estimates a 300:1 ratio of generated to final footage.
Footage was graded, edited, stabilised and mostly upscaled.
Sora clips often looked like slow motion and had to be retimed.
Recurring objects such as a banana came out different each time, so every detail was re-described in each prompt.

sources.title: Air Head production write-up (Chinese, from the fxguide interview)
claims: About 90 seconds of final cut came from hundreds of clips, a ratio near 300:1.
Each render took 10-20 minutes; shots were made at 480p and upscaled with Topaz to save time.
Grain and flicker were added to tie shots together; a camera tilt was faked by rendering portrait and cropping in post.
Prompt details such as 35 mm film helped balloon colour consistency.
sources.notes: Secondary translation of the fxguide interview; original not opened.

sources.title: How to make a short film with AI: the full pipeline
claims: Order: script breakdown, train character IDs, storyboard stills, shots, audio per scene, edit.
Storyboard each scene as 4-8 stills before generating its shots; fixing blocking after video exists means regenerating.
Generate the hardest shot of a scene first; if it holds, the rest usually will.
Keep clips short and chain at matching frames; identity and lighting degrade past about 30 seconds.
Quoted costs: about $3.75 per 8 s 720p shot, $7.50 per 15 s 1080p shot; a 5-minute short about $150.
sources.notes: Vendor pricing.

sources.title: AI storyboard generator: plan ads, demos and short films
claims: Turn the idea into one sentence, then a small set of visual beats; give each shot a single job.
Define visual rules (aspect ratio, palette, lens feel, recurring props) before generating.
Generate short tests and review continuity before producing the full sequence.
sources.notes: Competitor-neutral method, vendor blog.

sources.title: Topaz Astra: video creative upscale (ComfyUI workflow)
claims: Upscalers: Fast, Creative (adds detail) and Precise 2.5 (closest to source); output 1080p or 4K.
apo-8 interpolation can smooth motion; a creativity level of low, middle or high limits invented detail.
One video per run; the API version is paid and the page warns against auto-retrying a submission of unknown outcome.

sources.title: Across Every Universe: how I built an AI film from zero
claims: Built all character, location and prop references first, then storyboarded every scene and used panel crops as start frames.
Chained clips so each last frame becomes the next first frame; breaking the chain makes the character drift.
Matched tool to shot (Kling for dialogue and camera, Seedance for faces) and edited continuously in DaVinci Resolve.
A text prompt could not override a strong reference: an image with three monitors kept three monitors.
Two scenes failed or were abandoned: multi-character dialogue with a style, and symmetric two-character blocking.
Claims one hour of reference work saves about five hours of generation.
sources.notes: Final film 2 min 35 s; no totals given.

sources.title: What I learned after creating dozens of AI videos
claims: Design characters as stills from several angles first, then a start (and often end) image per scene.
Pick one camera move per scene; keep clips 6-10 seconds, six to eight clips per video.
Replacing one weak short clip is cheaper than rebuilding a whole video; edit last.
Viewers forgive style but not contradiction between shots.

sources.title: 47 failed renders chasing the air bending effect: a postmortem
claims: 47 renders cost $73.40; the author thinks about 14 would have sufficed with batching.
Serial one-prompt-one-output judging fails because run-to-run variance can exceed prompt-to-prompt variance.
Fix: four variations per prompt judged as a set, one prompt each for setup, effect and payoff, lock winners like version control.
Suggests a 25-30 percent throwaway rate as healthy; above 40 percent the shot definition is too vague.
sources.notes: Author discloses an affiliate link.

sources.title: Why AI video credits run out
claims: Expect about 3-10 generations per usable clip; real cost per clip is one generation times attempts.
A 10 s 1080p take costs about four times a 5 s 720p draft.
Draft on lighter model versions and keep the premium model for final renders; check exact credit cost first.
Camera and lighting left to text get reinterpreted each attempt; use controls or references instead.
sources.notes: Vendor blog.

sources.title: How many AI video credits do you need to make a short
claims: One animated episode: 164 clips generated, 41 used (25 percent), about 3 generations per usable shot, about 5 s kept of each 15 s clip.
A 90-second horror short took about 400 video generations.
Documented productions cost $315-$750 per finished minute over 2-5 days.
Plan 3-5x the final runtime in footage; approve images before spending video credits.
sources.notes: Vendor FAQ; its own production figures.

sources.title: LTX-2.5 workflow in ComfyUI
claims: First-last-frame uses the image and last_frame inputs; use the same aspect ratio for both for smooth interpolation.
Pro supports 2-10 s, Fast 2-20 s; over 10 s needs 720p or 1080p at 24 or 25 fps.
Fast is the default for image-to-video iteration; switch to Pro for quality.
Write the scene as one flowing paragraph and say what happens next from the start image.

sources.title: Behind ANCESTRA: combining Veo with live-action filmmaking
claims: A team of over 200 people made it; AI-generated shots were combined with live action through storyboards, VFX compositing and colour grading.
A fine-tuned Imagen model kept art direction consistent; Veo animated the images and could copy camera motion from a draft shot.
Challenges: matching quality and colour to live action, and controlling camera and performance from text alone.

sources.title: How to build a complete storyline with AI video
claims: Loop: outline, style frames, text-to-video draft, multi-element revision, then batch derivatives.
Treat the first render as a baseline and run 3-5 light passes with different seeds, then shortlist the strongest takes.
Lock reference images for characters and locations early; keep scene IDs in prompts for continuity.
sources.notes: Vendor guide.

sources.title: What does an AI film post-production pipeline look like
claims: Order: conform and log, continuity/artifact check, rough assembly act by act, upscale then grade, audio, final QC.
About 40 percent of final shots were composites of two or more generations.
Seedance output can look over-sharp and plasticky: add slight blur, grain and a grade toward live action.
Calls the final full-playthrough QC the step most people skip.
sources.notes: Vendor FAQ.

sources.title: Realistic clip discard rate for AI film
claims: Realistic discard rate is 70-80 percent of generated clips.
Multi-character physical contact, POV and continuity-heavy shots break far more often than simple single-character shots.
Budget by total generated seconds; each 15 s generation holds 4-7 shot candidates.
17 final shots were composited from the best seconds of several generations of one prompt.
sources.notes: Vendor FAQ.

sources.title: Firefly Boards and Generative Extend in Premiere Pro
claims: Firefly Boards holds shots as cards with prompt, reference, model and aspect ratio, and sends approved generations to Premiere.
Generative Extend adds at most 2 s of video at one clip end, will not make dialogue, and is 8-bit SDR.
Generated shots tend to drift warm and low in contrast against camera footage; match exposure and skin tones.
Use cheaper models for ideation and premium ones for finals.
sources.notes: Unverified against Adobe release notes.

sources.title: Runway Academy tutorials
claims: Lists a storyboard creator workflow, a character creator workflow, Story Panels for building a world from one reference, and Gen-4 References including 3D assets.
Lists Aleph tools for next shot, new angles and environment changes, and Act-Two for performance and voice change.
Includes making-of tutorials for the short films Grizzlies and Flicker.
sources.notes: Index page only; the tutorials themselves were not read.

sources.title: Colour grading AI video in DaVinci Resolve
claims: Upscale before colour work so the grade does not shift afterward.
Same node order on every clip: balance, match, look, texture; pick a hero clip and match others on the waveform and vectorscope.
Apply blur, uniform grain and optional halation as one texture pass; add LUTs last, never to match clips.
The free version of Resolve covers the whole workflow.
sources.notes: Vendor tutorial.

sources.title: Wan2.2 README
claims: TI2V-5B makes 720p at 24 fps and needs at least 24 GB VRAM; the 14B models need about 80 GB for single-GPU commands.
Authors say TI2V-5B produces a 5 second 720p clip in under 9 minutes on one consumer GPU.
Image-to-video output aspect ratio follows the input image; prompt extension is recommended.
sources.notes: Read from the raw README; first-last-frame not covered there.

sources.title: LTX-Video README (legacy 0.9.x)
claims: Supports image-to-video, multi-keyframe conditioning and video extension; each condition has a target frame and a strength (default 1.0).
Resolution should be divisible by 32 and frame count 8n+1; works best under 720x1280 and 257 frames.
Distilled models allow fast iteration, with 8 steps recommended.
Prompt as one chronological paragraph under 200 words, like a cinematographer.
sources.notes: Repo recommends the newer LTX-2.5 for new work.

sources.title: Sora is finicky: hundreds of generations and VFX for under two minutes
claims: Air Head took nearly two weeks, mostly because of Sora limits.
About 300:1 generated to final footage, so roughly 0.33 percent made the cut.
Extra heads, balloon faces and strings were removed in After Effects; the edit used a found-footage style because shots lacked cohesion.
The script was adapted to what the model produced.

sources.title: Veo API pricing
claims: Gemini API per second: Veo 3.1 $0.40 (720p/1080p), $0.60 at 4K; Fast $0.10-$0.30; Lite $0.05-$0.08.
An 8 second 1080p Veo 3.1 clip costs $3.20; no free tier.
sources.notes: Price read 2026-10-13 by the aggregator; check Google for current rates.

sources.title: OpenArt shifts to end-to-end storytelling
claims: OpenArt folds scripting, storyboards, character consistency, scenes, audio and assembly into one flow (One-Click Story, Director).
A saved character can be reused across scenes and across videos.
Video generation uses far more credits than images.
sources.notes: Analyst summary, not OpenArt docs.

sources.title: How to make a film with AI: complete workflow with prompts
claims: Eight steps: script, shot list, characters, look frames, shots, voice, fixes, edit; assemble, grade and upscale only after the cut is locked.
Shot list columns: shot number, scene, size, camera move, lens feel, duration 3-15 s, characters, key action, continuity notes; one action per shot.
Shot prompt has four parts (subject/action, camera, lens/light, duration); change one variable between takes.
Approve script, shot list, character sheets and look frames before generating; a fix prompt changes one thing and keeps the rest.

sources.title: Kling 3 multi-shot storyboard tutorial
claims: Up to 6 cuts and 15 seconds per generation; write each cut with size, action, camera and explicit duration.
A 5-10 second reference clip with a well-lit face locks identity better than one still.
If lip sync drifts, regenerate the whole sequence; audio added after rendering breaks alignment.
Iterate on Standard, upgrade only the final generation to Pro; a 15 s clip with audio costs about $1.12-$2.94.
